name: Electron main process built as an Effect layer graph with staged startup
what: The desktop shell is assembled as a typed dependency graph of services instead of imperative event handlers. Startup, fatal errors and shutdown follow an explicit sequence, so a failure at any stage shows one error dialog and a clean quit.
how: main.ts merges Layers for every Electron API wrapped as a service (ElectronApp, ElectronWindow, ElectronDialog, ElectronUpdater, ElectronSafeStorage, ElectronProtocol, ElectronPowerMonitor, ElectronTheme, DesktopIpc over ipcMain) plus foundation, backend-pool, WSL, SSH, updates and Clerk layers, then runs DesktopApp.program with NodeRuntime.runMain. startup() runs: shell-environment import, userData path, settings load, lifecycle register, Clerk configure, whenReady, menu, updates, Linux URL handler, then bootstrap (port selection, exposure config, protocol registration, IPC handlers, backend start). Fatal errors at whenReady or bootstrap call handleFatalStartupError (log, error box, shutdown request, quit). A scoped finalizer stops every backend in the pool concurrently so none is hard-killed.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's Rust gateway can copy the idea of wrapping every platform capability behind an injectable service interface with an explicit startup/shutdown DAG, which makes each stage testable and fail-loud.
notes: Depends on Effect 4.0.0-beta.103 (pre-release) throughout; the pattern ports to Rust traits/actors, the library does not. Quality 4 because the staging is clean but the beta dependency is a maintenance risk.

name: One server artifact, many hosting shells (desktop, headless, SSH, WSL, boot service)
what: The same Node server bundle powers the desktop app, a headless `t3 serve`, a remote machine reached over SSH, a WSL distro, and a systemd/launchd boot service. The shells only differ in how they bootstrap and supervise it.
how: ServerConfig.mode is 'web' or 'desktop'; the desktop passes a one-time bootstrap envelope (DesktopBackendBootstrap) and the CLI flag --bootstrap-fd. The desktop never embeds UI: the SPA lives in server.asar and is served by the backend. SSH sends a launcher script that runs `serve --host 127.0.0.1` on the remote box; WSL runs `wsl.exe --exec node bin.mjs`; the boot service points a unit/plist at a pinned runtime directory.
verevonRelevance: Verevon already separates a Rust gateway from the SolidJS SPA; the lesson is to keep one server artifact and make every deployment shape (cloud, on-prem, local dev) a thin bootstrap difference rather than a fork.
notes: The scout noted the thin-shell layout; this record adds the multiplicity of shells and the bootstrap contract.

name: Privileged t3code://app scheme that reverse-proxies the UI to the backend with an injected CSP
what: The Electron window loads a custom secure origin instead of http://localhost:<port>, so the renderer origin stays stable while the backend port changes. Every response gets a Content-Security-Policy header.
how: registerSchemesAsPrivileged marks t3code (and t3code-dev) standard, secure, fetch-capable and CORS-enabled before ready. protocol.handle proxies any request on host 'app' to the backend origin with Electron.net.fetch, strips host/origin/referer/sec-fetch headers, retries GET/HEAD at 0/50/150 ms, then rewrites the response with a CSP built by makeDesktopContentSecurityPolicy (script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' plus Clerk and Cloudflare challenge origins, connect-src limited only by scheme http/https/ws/wss).
verevonRelevance: A web chat app can reuse the idea of one stable origin plus a response-level CSP injected at the edge (Verevon's Rust gateway) instead of relying on per-page meta tags.
notes: The CSP is permissive by design (inline scripts, any http(s)/ws(s) connect target) because the renderer must reach user-configured environments; treat that as a trade-off, not a model for a multi-tenant SaaS.

name: Backend child-process protocol: fd-3 bootstrap, readiness probe, SIGTERM-then-kill, restart backoff
what: The desktop supervises its embedded server like a service. Secrets are passed without argv or env, readiness is probed over HTTP, crashes restart with backoff and unrecoverable preflight failures stop the loop with a visible reason.
how: The server is spawned with process.execPath plus ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1, args [entry, --bootstrap-fd, 3]. The bootstrap JSON line (port, host, home, one-time desktopBootstrapToken, tailscale flags, OTLP URLs, telemetry fds 4/5, resource-monitor path) is written to an extra fd (stdin for WSL, because wsl.exe drops extra fds). Output is captured to rotating logs. waitForHttpReady polls /.well-known/t3/environment (100 ms interval, 1 s request timeout, 1 min budget). Exit triggers restart with delay from 500 ms up to 10 s; preflight failures flagged fatal stop after 5 attempts and call onPreflightFailed; transient failures (WSL cold start) retry. Stop sends SIGTERM and force-kills after 2 s.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's compose/runner supervision of Rust and Go services could adopt the same split between fatal and transient preflight failures plus a bounded restart loop that surfaces a reason instead of spinning.
notes: Credential handoff via an inherited fd (not argv/env) is the right shape for any parent-child secret passing.

name: Backend instance factory and pool (primary plus WSL) with per-instance logs
what: Several backends can run side by side. Each has its own state, mutex, restart loop, log file and lifecycle callbacks; only the primary drives window readiness.
how: makeBackendInstance(spec) builds an isolated lifecycle (state Ref, Semaphore, restart fiber, child process). DesktopBackendPool registers/unregisters instances in child scopes; the primary id refuses unregister. Config comes from a per-instance configResolve closure (resolvePrimary vs resolveWsl). Log writers are keyed by instance id (server-child.log vs server-child-<id>.log). The design header documents the 10-commit migration from a singleton manager.
verevonRelevance: Useful as a template for a per-tenant or per-sandbox worker supervisor in Verevon: one factory, isolated state, shared pool registry.
notes: The file header records design decisions and a migration history, which is rare and valuable (DOC-quality commentary inside SRC).

name: Typed RPC over WebSocket with one shared contracts package for client and server
what: All interactive traffic (commands, queries, subscriptions) rides one WebSocket using Effect RPC; HTTP is used only for snapshots, attachments, assets, OTLP and auth. Client and server are generated from the same method group, so version drift is a compile error.
how: packages/contracts defines WS_METHODS and ORCHESTRATION_WS_METHODS (97 plus 8 method names in the tables; 17 stream-typed definitions in rpc.ts plus the two orchestration subscriptions, for about 19 streaming methods) as Rpc.make groups; the server mounts them with RpcServer and RpcSerialization.layerJson; the client builds RpcClient.make(WsRpcGroup). The Bun/Node HTTP server negotiates permessage-deflate (dedicated compressor with context takeover on Bun). A wsTicket query parameter (5 min TTL) authenticates the upgrade because browsers cannot set headers on WebSocket.
verevonRelevance: Verevon uses HTTP+SSE at the edge and gRPC internally; a typed bidirectional channel for the chat/agent page (approvals, interrupts, subscriptions) would remove the SSE-plus-POST split, and sharing one schema source keeps Rust and the SPA honest.
notes: Wire format is JSON (msgpackr is a dependency but RPC uses layerJson). Correction to the scout: msgpackr is not the RPC codec.

name: Connection supervisor with four target kinds, backoff and application wake-ups
what: The client can connect to the local backend, a paired remote server by bearer token, a managed relay, or an SSH tunnel, all through one supervised connection state machine that reconnects when the app wakes or the network changes.
how: client-runtime defines tagged targets (PrimaryConnectionTarget, BearerConnectionTarget, RelayConnectionTarget, SshConnectionTarget). ConnectionDriver.connect runs prepare, opening, synchronizing (session.ready). ConnectionSupervisor reacts to signals (ConnectRequested, DisconnectRequested, RetryRequested, NetworkChanged, Wakeup) with delays of 3, 4, 8 and 16 s, a 15 s establishment timeout, a 3 s probe on mobile, and resets backoff after 30 s of stability. Wakeups (application-active, -probe, -reconnect, credentials-changed) decide whether subscriptions are re-opened.
verevonRelevance: The Verevon SPA's SSE reconnection could adopt an explicit supervisor state machine with wake-up reasons (tab visible, credentials changed) instead of ad-hoc retries.
notes: A mobile client is in the monorepo (Expo/React Native overrides in pnpm config) and shares this runtime; it is not in this build.

name: Event-sourced single-writer command engine with receipts and transactional projections
what: Every UI action is a command processed one at a time. Accepted commands produce events, update read models and store a receipt in a single SQL transaction, so retries are idempotent and a replayed command id cannot report success for work aimed at a different aggregate.
how: OrchestrationEngine owns an unbounded Queue of CommandEnvelope and a worker fiber. For each command: look up the receipt (same id but other aggregate gives OrchestrationCommandIdConflictError; accepted returns the stored sequence; rejected gives PreviouslyRejected); run the pure decider against the in-memory command read model; stamp client origin on events; in sql.withTransaction append each event, project it in memory, run the projection pipeline, and upsert an accepted receipt; then publish to a PubSub (each consumer gets its own subscription). On failure the read model is reconciled from the event store and an invariant failure is persisted as a rejected receipt.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's session-core is already the single writer for threads/runs; adding command receipts with an aggregate-mismatch check and reconcile-after-failure would harden retries from the SPA and from reactors.
notes: The sibling UI audit covers the client sync side (its record 091); this record is the server write path. Weakness: the queue is process-local and unbounded, fine for single-user, not for multi-replica.

name: Command tiers and intent-event reactors
what: Clients may only dispatch a fixed subset of commands; server-only commands (assistant deltas, session state, activity append, diff completion, revert completion) are internal. Side effects run in reactors that listen for requested-style intent events and report back by dispatching internal commands.
how: contracts split DispatchableClientOrchestrationCommand, ClientOrchestrationCommand and InternalOrchestrationCommand unions. ProviderCommandReactor handles thread.meta-updated, runtime-mode-set, turn-start-requested, turn-interrupt-requested, approval-response-requested, user-input-response-requested and session-stop-requested. ProviderRuntimeIngestion turns provider runtime events into internal commands; CheckpointReactor, ThreadDeletionReactor and RuntimeReceiptBus complete the set; all are layered in ReactorLayerLive.
verevonRelevance: Directly applicable to Verevon's session-core/gateway split: make the client-callable command set a closed schema and drive provider calls from intent events so approvals, interrupts and restarts are all auditable events.
notes: Separating the 'requested' event from the 'happened' event is what makes crash recovery and the activity timeline simple.

name: Projection pipeline with nine resumable projectors
what: Read models (projects, messages, plans, activities, sessions, turns, checkpoints, pending approvals, threads) are separate projectors that each remember the last event sequence they applied, so a restart or a new projector replays only what it missed.
how: ORCHESTRATION_PROJECTOR_NAMES lists the nine projectors; projectEvent runs them sequentially per event for deterministic ordering and writes lastAppliedSequence into projection state; bootstrap resumes each projector from its stored cursor before the engine starts accepting commands.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's Postgres-backed session-core could adopt per-projector cursors so new views (search, usage, activity feeds) are added by replay instead of backfill scripts.
notes: The read side carries most of the code (ProjectionPipeline about 1.8k lines, ProjectionSnapshotQuery about 2.9k lines).

name: SQLite in WAL mode with dual Bun/Node drivers and in-place payload migrations
what: State lives in one SQLite file with 43 ordered migrations. The server and the CLI can write from separate processes without lock errors. Event payloads are patched in place by SQL migrations when schemas change.
how: makeRuntimeSqliteLayer picks @effect/sql-sqlite-bun or a NodeSqliteClient at runtime; setup runs PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000, foreign_keys=ON, journal_mode=WAL then runMigrations. Migration 001 creates orchestration_events with a unique (aggregate_kind, stream_id, stream_version) index; later migrations backfill projections and rewrite event payload_json via json_set/json_remove (011 adds a default runtimeMode to thread.created events; 016 rewrites model selections).
verevonRelevance: Verevon uses Postgres, so the transferable part is the stream_version unique index for optimistic concurrency per aggregate; the in-place event rewrite is a pattern to avoid in favour of versioned upcasters.
notes: Rewriting stored events breaks the 'events are immutable' guarantee and makes replay-from-zero depend on migration order. Acceptable for a local single-user store.

name: Staged server startup: parked roots, activation gate, command-readiness gate, orphan-session reconcile
what: The server brings up long-running roots in a parked state and releases them only after the HTTP listener and runtime state are ready; HTTP requests wait until commands can be accepted; sessions that died with the previous process are marked as errors with an explanation.
how: forkParked forks a fiber that signals it is parked then waits on a ServerActivation deferred. makeServerLayer wires parked layers (runtime-state file, Tailscale Serve, cloud link, reactors). commandReadinessLayer is a global HTTP middleware that awaits startup.awaitCommandReady; ws dispatch uses startup.enqueueCommand. reconcileProviderSessions compares persisted bindings and thread sessions in starting/running/active-turn state against live provider sessions and, for orphans, marks the binding stopped and dispatches thread.session.set with status error and a message that the session did not survive a restart.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's gateway already drains on /readyz; the orphan-session reconcile step (mark in-flight runs as errored with a human message on boot) is a cheap, user-visible reliability win.
notes: Pairs with the managed-run terminalization/recovery worker already in Verevon session-core.

name: Headless server self-update: pinned runtimes, preflight, launcher trial child and database rollback
what: A headless T3 server can update itself on remote request. The new version is installed beside the old one, checked, started as a trial against a snapshot of the database, and either committed or rolled back automatically.
how: ServerSelfUpdate (capability 'boot-service' only when run under the launcher; 'desktop-managed' refuses) installs the exact t3@version into <baseDir>/runtime/versions/<v> under an install lock with a completion sentinel, then runs `__service-preflight --database-path ... --launcher-protocol 2` (30 s) and verifies the reported version. It then asks the service launcher (a separate service-launcher.mjs supervisor with an IPC protocol v2) to activate the update. The launcher records a pending update in service-state.json, stops the active child, snapshots state.sqlite plus -wal and -shm once, starts the target as a 'trial' child, and commits only when the trial reports 'prepared'; a 120 s timeout, a crash, a missing runtime or a failed backup returns to the previous version and restores the database (a .restore-pending marker protects an interrupted restore). Stop grace is 5 s, handoff delay 2 s. Progress streams to the client over server.updateServerWithProgress.
verevonRelevance: For a Rust-and-Go control plane the transferable idea is blue/green with a database snapshot and an automatic commit-or-rollback decision based on the new version reporting healthy; Verevon's signed-artifact runner could add a preflight command that validates migrations before cutover.
notes: The launcher source was recovered from service-launcher.mjs.map (extracted to tmp/t3arch/src/serviceLauncher.ts). Supported only on Linux systemd and macOS launchd; the Windows status text says unavailable. SQLite snapshotting is trivial; it would not carry over to a shared Postgres.

name: Desktop auto-update is user-driven, channel-aware and stops all backends before install
what: The app checks for updates in the background but never downloads or installs without the user. Stable and nightly channels are supported, and installing shuts every backend down gracefully first.
how: electron-updater is configured with autoDownload=false and autoInstallOnAppQuit=false; a first check runs 15 s after start, then every 4 minutes. The channel is derived from the app version (a -nightly.YYYYMMDD.N suffix means nightly); the nightly channel enables prerelease, downgrade and full changelog, a channel switch temporarily forces allowDowngrade for one held check (so moving from nightly to stable can land on an older stable build), and updates that do not match the selected channel are ignored. A pure reducer file (updateMachine.ts) models checking/available/downloading/downloaded/error with canRetry, and download failure keeps an 'available' state when a version is known. installUpdate stops all pool instances with a 5 s timeout, destroys windows, then quitAndInstall(silent, forceRunAfter). An Intel build on an Apple Silicon host disables differential download and switches to arm64 packages. Updates are disabled for dev builds, missing feed config, T3CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE and non-AppImage Linux.
verevonRelevance: Verevon is a web app and does not need an updater, but the client-version skew handling (see the capability-flag record) matters when the SPA and gateway deploy at different times.
notes: A 4-minute poll is aggressive for a GitHub releases feed; presumably cached by electron-updater. Release notes are fetched and parsed (releaseNotes.ts).

name: Capability flags in the environment descriptor for client/server version skew
what: Each server advertises which features it understands, so a newer desktop client connected to an older remote server hides or falls back instead of sending commands the server would reject.
how: GET /.well-known/t3/environment returns an ExecutionEnvironmentDescriptor with ExecutionEnvironmentCapabilities (optional booleans such as attachmentUploads, pullRequests, threadSettlement, threadSnooze, threadPinning, threadPinReorder, threadTitleRegeneration, threadPullRequestLinking, serverSelfUpdate, serverSelfUpdateProgress, agentActivityPublishing). Comments define the contract: a missing key means unsupported and the client must not probe. The same endpoint doubles as the desktop's readiness probe. Browser-automation hosts advertise their supported operations for mixed-version routing.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's SPA and Rust gateway ship independently; a descriptor of supported commands/events (rather than a version number) lets the SPA degrade per feature during rolling deploys.
notes: Pairs with the 'missing means unsupported' rule; the sibling UI audit noted capability gating in the pagination sync (its record 047).

name: Model catalog and price tables refreshed from the web outside the release cycle
what: Which models count as current (versus legacy) and what they cost are data files fetched at runtime, so a new model appears in the picker or in usage costs without shipping a release.
how: ModelManifest fetches apps/server/src/provider/model-manifest.json from raw.githubusercontent.com main (1 h TTL, 5 min retry gap after failure, 10 s timeout), validates it with a version-literal schema, prefers remote then the on-disk copy of the last fetch then the bundled copy, and drivers apply it before publishing snapshots. UsageService separately fetches LiteLLM's model_prices_and_context_window.json (24 h TTL, disk cache) and prices transcript tokens from it. A failed fetch never fails a provider check.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's inference-core routing and cost-core could load model capability and price tables from a signed, versioned data artifact with a bundled fallback instead of redeploying services.
notes: Trust boundary: the manifest and price table come from an unauthenticated branch of a public repo; the schema version gate limits breakage but not malicious values. The sibling audit found Claude catalogs are static and CLI-version gated, so this manifest only reclassifies, it does not discover.

name: Native Rust resource-monitor sidecar with a versioned JSON command protocol
what: Per-process CPU and memory telemetry for the server, its agents and terminals comes from a small bundled native helper instead of Node polling, with a handshake, history reads and automatic restart.
how: t3-resource-monitor.exe is a 390 KB x86-64 PE built with rustc and the sysinfo 0.39.3 and serde_json crates (REA strings: sysinfo windows process.rs, cpu.rs; JSON field names pid, ppid, cpuPercent, cpuTimeMs, cumulativeCpuTime, sidecarPid, sampleIntervalMs, externalProcesses; command enum variants configure, setExternalProcesses, setSampleInterval, setStreaming, sampleNow, readHistory, shutdown). The server's NativeTelemetryClient spawns it, checks a hello handshake and RESOURCE_MONITOR_PROTOCOL_VERSION (5 s), sends configure/setStreaming/setExternalProcesses commands, requests sampleNow (5 s) and readHistory (15 s), restarts with 500 ms to 10 s backoff and gives up after 5 failures in 60 s. Sample interval adapts to power state (1 s live, 5 s battery, 15 s constrained). Samples are categorized (server, server-child, provider-root, terminal-root, electron-main, electron-renderer, electron-gpu, electron-utility, resource-monitor, unknown-t3), and ResourceAttribution adds per-component logical I/O counters (bytes, counts, durations; for example the trace writer reports its flushes).
verevonRelevance: A good small model for a Rust sidecar: versioned stdio JSON protocol, handshake, bounded restart and an adaptive sample rate; Verevon's Rust services could ship the same pattern for sandbox resource accounting.
notes: REA tools used: open_binary, binary_overview (829 procedures, 531 strings, ev_c06e...), search_strings (ev_940e...); inspect_pe_resources was run earlier by the scout (ev_974d...). The scout left the implementation language unverified; it is Rust (rustc commit string and cargo registry paths in the binary). Only a Windows x64 build is shipped in this install.

name: Desktop-to-server host telemetry side channel (fd 4 and fd 5)
what: The Electron host feeds its power, lock, battery, thermal and idle state to the embedded server over inherited pipes, so the server can pause or slow background work when the machine is locked, on battery or throttled.
how: The bootstrap passes desktopTelemetryFd=4 (host to server JSON lines) and desktopTelemetryControlFd=5 (server to host control). DesktopTelemetryPublisher samples every 1 s live, 5 s on battery, 15 s constrained, with idle threshold 60 s and host-power events (locked, suspended, onBattery, thermal, speedLimit). The server's DesktopTelemetryReceiver decodes the stream, flags stale or closed streams and exposes HostPowerMonitor; clients can also report power with server.reportHostPowerState.
verevonRelevance: Mostly desktop-specific, but it shows how a host can lend context (power, idle) to a headless agent runtime; Verevon's browser client could report visibility/idle to the gateway to throttle runs and polling.
notes: No comparable side channel exists in the other desktop apps audited.

name: Demand-driven background work using client activity leases and power-aware policy
what: Polling work (git status, provider health, discovered dev servers, diagnostics) runs only while some connected client actually shows that data, and slows or pauses with host power state.
how: BackgroundPolicy tracks ClientActivityLease records per (session, RPC client, client) with a 45 s default and 120 s maximum TTL and at most 16 leases per RPC client; scopes are server-config, diagnostics, provider-status(instance), vcs-status(cwd), git-refs(cwd) and thread(id). Workers ask hasDemand/shouldRunScopeWork/shouldRunOpportunisticWork; settings pauseWhenOnBattery, pauseWhenHostLocked, pauseWhenHostLowPower, pauseWhenClientLowPower and active/idle intervals shape the answer. VcsStatusBroadcaster refreshes every 30 s with failure backoff up to 15 min; makeManagedServerProvider refreshes provider snapshots under the same policy; PortScanner polling is reference counted by retain.
verevonRelevance: Directly relevant to Verevon's multi-tenant cost: the gateway can hold per-scope demand leases from the SPA so watches, polling and provider health checks do not run for tabs nobody is viewing; it also gives a principled alternative to the process-local registries that limit multi-replica.
notes: Leases are in memory; a multi-replica Verevon would keep them in Redis/NATS with the same TTL semantics.

name: Atomic JSON persistence and keystore-encrypted desktop catalog versus plaintext server secret files
what: Desktop settings are written atomically and the saved-connection catalog (which holds bearer tokens) is encrypted with the OS keystore, but the server's own secret store keeps files in plaintext protected only by permissions.
how: Desktop settings, client settings and the connection catalog write to a temp file named with the pid and rename over the target; the catalog has explicit encrypt-catalog/decrypt-catalog steps (Electron safeStorage, with a Linux password-store selection step). The server's ServerSecretStore writes <secretsDir>/<name>.bin with flag 'wx' (exclusive create) or temp+rename, chmod 0700 on the directory and 0600 on files, and has no encryption code at all; it stores signing keys, DPoP replay markers, relay credentials, CLI OAuth tokens and the asset signing key.
verevonRelevance: Confirms the baseline for a hosted product: never keep tenant secrets as plain files; Verevon's envelope-encrypted continuation descriptors and secret handling are ahead of this on the server side.
notes: chmod has no effect on Windows NTFS, so on Windows these files rely on the user profile ACL. The scout flagged encryption at rest as unverified; zero encryption identifiers exist in ServerSecretStore.ts.

name: Login-shell and PowerShell environment hydration so GUI-launched agents find their CLIs
what: Apps started from the dock or Start menu do not inherit the user's shell PATH. T3 recovers it so the agent CLIs, git and package managers resolve the way they do in a terminal.
how: DesktopShellEnvironment probes in order: login shell (POSIX), launchctl path (macOS), PowerShell with profile, PowerShell without profile (Windows). The server repeats this in fixPath(): hydratePosixPath reads PATH from login-shell candidates (markers __T3CODE_PATH_START__/END__), merges with the process PATH, falls back to launchctl, and fills HOME; on Windows resolveWindowsEnvironment repairs the environment. Terminals strip PORT, ELECTRON_RENDERER_PORT and ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE from the spawned shell environment.
verevonRelevance: Relevant only to a local agent runtime; for Verevon's sandboxes the same lesson is to construct an explicit environment rather than inherit one.
notes: A tell-tale 'os-jank' file name: this is a long tail of per-OS workarounds.

name: Managed relay (T3 Connect): pinned cloudflared tunnel, environment-signed proofs and scoped links
what: A user can reach their own machine's server from a phone or the hosted web app without opening ports. The server links to a relay, receives a managed endpoint, and runs a Cloudflare tunnel connector; it can also publish agent-activity snapshots for push notifications and Live Activities.
how: RelayClient downloads a pinned cloudflared release per platform (2026.5.2) into the base dir, verifies SHA-256 against a pinned table ('invalid_checksum' otherwise) under an install lock with a 5 min stale-lock timeout, and CloudManagedEndpointRuntime runs it as a child process classifying its log lines. The link is an OAuth-style flow with environment-signed JWT proofs (EnvironmentLinkProofPayload with challenge, descriptor, public key, endpoint, scopes agent_activity_notifications and managed_tunnels); endpoint kinds are manual, cloudflare_tunnel and t3_relay. AgentAwarenessRelay projects thread shells to RelayAgentActivityState (titles, phase, headline, model, deep link) and publishes only on lifecycle events that change the authoritative state, signed with an environment key pair stored in the secret store.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's Channel Plane is docs-only; this shows a minimal, privacy-preserving notification payload (titles and phase only, no message content) and a signed-proof link model that Channel Plane could copy for mobile alerts.
notes: The connect command reports 'unavailable in builds without public configuration', so the relay path needs a build with public config. Provider tokens and message text are not in the published state schema.

name: Three auth policies, one-time pairing, scoped bearer sessions and DPoP proof-of-possession
what: A server decides how strictly to authenticate based on how it is exposed: desktop-managed local, loopback browser, or remote-reachable. Remote clients pair with short one-time tokens and then use scoped sessions, optionally bound to a device key with DPoP.
how: EnvironmentAuthPolicy selects the policy from mode and bind host and advertises bootstrap methods (desktop-bootstrap, one-time-token) and session methods (browser-session-cookie, bearer-access-token, dpop-access-token). Pairing tokens are 12 characters from an unambiguous alphabet with a 5 minute TTL (desktop bootstrap and dev startup tokens 24 h); sessions default to 30 days; WebSocket tickets 5 minutes. verifyRequestDpopProof validates the DPoP header against method, URL, expected thumbprint and access token, then records a hash of thumbprint+jti in the secret store with exclusive create so a replayed proof is rejected. HTTP routes cover pairing links, client list/revoke, revoke-others and an /oauth/token endpoint.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's Control Plane owns identity, but DPoP-bound sessions and one-time pairing for the future Channel Plane or desktop companions are a ready pattern.
notes: Single-user trust model: all scopes belong to one operator. There is no org, role or audit model.

name: Exhaustive RPC scope table enforced by the type system
what: Every WebSocket RPC method must declare the auth scope it needs; forgetting one is a compile error rather than an open endpoint.
how: RPC_REQUIRED_SCOPES is a total map keyed by the method names of WsRpcGroup, with scopes such as orchestration read, orchestration operate, terminal operate, review write, relay read/write and access read. Reads and writes are split deliberately (for example pullRequests.invalidate is read, request-reviewers is operate; terminal and review have their own scopes).
verevonRelevance: Verevon's gateway routes could adopt a generated, total route-to-scope table (Rust match over a route enum) so every new endpoint must state its tenant and scope requirement at compile time.
notes: Sensitive RPCs such as server.signalProcess and projects.writeFile require only the operate scope; there is no per-path or per-process authorization inside a scope.

name: Telemetry is on by default and the identity is hashed from the user's provider account
what: Anonymous analytics are enabled unless disabled by environment. The installation identifier is derived by hashing the Codex account id or Claude user id found in the provider CLIs' own config files, falling back to a random id.
how: AnalyticsService reads T3CODE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED with default true, buffers events and sends to PostHog. getTelemetryIdentifierForHome prefers SHA-256 of the account id in the Codex auth file, then of the Claude user id, then of a generated anonymous id file. Events include client surface and app version origin properties.
verevonRelevance: Avoid: Verevon's ZDR and tenancy promises are incompatible with identifying users by reading third-party account files; any product analytics must be opt-in and tenant-scoped.
notes: Resolves a scout open question: the default is enabled. The code reads the account id field only to hash it; no token values are used. This audit did not read any user files.

name: Server exposure modes with LAN binding and Tailscale Serve advertised endpoints
what: A desktop-managed server is loopback-only by default. The user can switch it to network-accessible (LAN bind) or enable Tailscale Serve and the app computes which URLs to show other devices.
how: DesktopServerExposure resolves mode local-only (127.0.0.1) or network-accessible (0.0.0.0 with an advertised LAN host from network interfaces or an override); it falls back to local-only with a warning when no advertised host exists. Tailscale status is read via the tailscale CLI (60 s cache), MagicDNS names and 100.x IPv4 addresses become advertised endpoint providers; the server itself runs ensureTailscaleServe on a parked layer and disables it on release. Changing the mode (or Tailscale Serve) triggers lifecycle.relaunch when a relaunch is required, so the backend restarts with the new bind host.
verevonRelevance: Not a hosted-product concern, but 'advertised endpoints' (a typed list of how this instance can be reached, with provider labels) is a useful descriptor for any multi-endpoint deployment.
notes: The bind is plain HTTP on the LAN; protection comes from pairing and scoped sessions.

name: Contract-first generated protocol clients for the Codex app-server and ACP
what: T3 does not hand-write the wire types for the agents it drives. Two internal packages are generated from the upstream protocol schemas and expose typed request, notification and server-request handlers over stdio.
how: effect-codex-app-server holds a 43k-line generated schema plus meta.gen.ts listing 87 client request methods (thread/*, turn/start|steer|interrupt, review/start, skills/*, plugin/*, marketplace/*, fs/*, command/exec*, mcpServer/*, account/*, config/*), 8 server requests (approvals, user input, MCP elicitation, tool call, token refresh, attestation) and 67 server notifications; CodexAppServerClient registers typed handlers and an unknown-method fallback. effect-acp is generated for ACP schema v0.11.3 (14 agent methods, 11 client methods) over JSON-RPC on stdio. T3 itself calls only about ten Codex methods today (initialize, thread/start|resume|read|rollback, turn/start|interrupt, skills/list, model/list, config/mcpServer/reload, account/read, feedback/upload).
verevonRelevance: Verevon already routes to the user's ChatGPT subscription via Integration Core's Codex app-server; generating the Rust client from the same published JSON schema (as T3 does for TypeScript) would remove hand-maintained types and expose turn/steer, thread/rollback and plugin/skill methods.
notes: Method counts are from meta.gen.ts line ranges 6-100, 105-117 and 118-192. T3 leaves most of the Codex surface (plugins, marketplace, fs, steer, review) unused.

name: Desktop IPC surface: 101 channel operations behind an 86-member desktopBridge
what: The renderer talks to Electron main through one context-isolated bridge object with typed, schema-decoded handlers. A static analysis of the shipped preload scripts confirms how large the surface is and that it includes Clerk's token, OAuth and passkey bridges.
how: REA analyze_javascript_application on apps/desktop/dist-electron (8 JS files, 170,657 AST nodes) found 4 contextBridge APIs (desktopBridge with 86 members, previewPictureInPicture with 1, and two Clerk bridges), 101 IPC channel operations (78 invoke, 4 sendSync, 5 send, 14 listeners) all with identifier-based channel names, 14 renderer listeners and no resolvable main-process handlers. Cross-checking the 83 *_CHANNEL constants in ipc/channels.ts shows every one appears in the preload; the remaining 15 channels belong to Clerk (token cache get/save/clear, OAuth transport open/getRedirectUrl, passkeys create/get/capabilities) and to the preview element-picker preload (element picked, annotation captured, human input, mouse navigate). Main registers handlers through DesktopIpc.makeIpcMethod, which pairs each channel with a payload Schema, a result Schema and a handler Effect (decode, run with a span and log annotations, encode), so validation and error handling are centralized; synchronous channels use makeSyncIpcMethod.
verevonRelevance: None directly for a web app; it documents how much native surface a desktop shell needs (folder pickers, SSH, WSL, updates, browser preview), which is the cost Verevon avoids by staying web-only.
notes: REA could not resolve literal channel strings (dynamic identifiers) and found 0 main handlers (main.cjs semantic graph exceeded the result budget), so the main-side map comes from SRC. A trace_application_feature call with an api seed 'exposeInMainWorld' returned no match (ev_902fca7c...); a module seed on 'preload.cjs' produced the graph used here (result saved under tmp/t3arch/rea_trace_preload.json).

name: Hardened window and guarded preview webviews
what: The main window runs sandboxed with context isolation, blocks navigation to other origins, and only allows webviews on T3's own browser partitions; guest pages get a sandbox but no Node.
how: BrowserWindow webPreferences set contextIsolation true, nodeIntegration false, sandbox true, webviewTag true. will-attach-webview rejects any partition not created by the preview manager and forces sandbox true, nodeIntegration false, nodeIntegrationInSubFrames false (contextIsolation false in the guest so the Playwright injected runtime and react-grab can run in the page world). setWindowOpenHandler denies all new windows and opens only safe external URLs in the OS browser; will-navigate blocks anything but same-origin renderer navigation; ElectronShell.parseSafeExternalUrl only lets http(s)-style web protocols and vscode-remote editor URLs reach shell.openExternal. Preview sessions use persistent partitions with the prefix persist:t3code-preview-<scope>.
verevonRelevance: Reference checklist for Verevon's manual-browser/Quarry live view if it ever embeds third-party pages: partition per scope, deny window.open, same-origin navigation only.
notes: Guest contextIsolation=false means page scripts can see the injected globals (for example __t3PlaywrightInjected).

name: Instant connecting splash and window readiness following the primary backend
what: In WSL-only mode a lightweight 'Connecting to WSL' window appears immediately while the slow backend boots; in normal mode the real window opens as soon as the primary backend reports ready and re-opens if it restarts.
how: DesktopWindow keeps a readiness latch driven by the pool's onReady/onShutdown callbacks, loads the application URL once ready, and reveals on ready-to-show. A data-URL splash with a strict CSP is created when settings say wslOnly and wslBackendEnabled, tracked in its own ref, closed once the real window is revealed, and re-revealed on dock activation if the backend is still not ready. The window follows only the primary backend.
verevonRelevance: For the web app the equivalent is a skeleton or connecting state that appears before the Model Plane stream is ready, with an explicit reason when it is slow.
notes: A Chrome-style hold-to-quit (1200 ms hold, 500 ms double tap) lives in window/QuitHold.ts; it is UI polish with some risk for keyboards without auto-repeat (falls back to the menu).

name: ProviderDriver SPI: drivers as plain values, instances as captured closures, hot-reloadable registry
what: Each supported agent (Claude, Codex, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode) is a driver value that can be instantiated many times with its own config. An instance bundles a status snapshot source, a session adapter and a text-generation capability; settings changes add or remove instances without a restart.
how: ProviderDriver has driverKind, metadata (displayName, supportsMultipleInstances), configSchema (decoded once by the registry), defaultConfig and create(input) that returns a ProviderInstance {instanceId, driverKind, continuationIdentity, displayName, accentColor, enabled, snapshot, adapter, textGeneration}. There are deliberately no per-driver Context tags, so two Codex accounts share no mutable state. ProviderInstanceRegistryHydration merges legacy settings.providers.<kind> with explicit providerInstances; ProviderAdapterRegistryLive is a facade that resolves adapters from the registry on every call, so hot reload shows up immediately; decode failures become 'unavailable shadow' snapshots instead of defects. BUILT_IN_DRIVERS lists the static set.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's inference-core routes across Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere and the Codex subscription route; a driver/instance split with per-instance config schema and continuation identity would formalize multi-account and BYOK routing without singleton services.
notes: The sibling UI audit covers how the UI consumes instances (its records 001-003); this record is the server-side SPI. The adapter interface file (Services/ProviderAdapter.ts) is type-only and was erased from the source map; its shape is inferred from ProviderService and the adapters (startSession, sendTurn, interruptTurn, respondToRequest, respondToUserInput, stopSession, listSessions, hasSession, rollbackThread, readThread, plus capabilities).

name: Multi-account provider isolation: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR homes and Codex auth-overlay shadow homes
what: A user can run two accounts of the same agent side by side. Claude instances are isolated by config directory; Codex instances can share sessions, skills and plugins while keeping a private login.
how: makeClaudeEnvironment sets CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR for an instance homePath instead of overriding HOME (overriding HOME breaks the macOS keychain lookup), and makeClaudeContinuationGroupKey = claude:home:<path>. For Codex, resolveCodexHomeLayout returns mode 'direct' or 'authOverlay': with a shadowHomePath it builds a shadow directory that symlinks the shared directories (sessions, archived_sessions, sqlite, shell_snapshots, worktrees, skills, plugins, cache, logs, mcp-oauth-locks) to the shared home while auth.json and models_cache.json stay private and log/memories/tmp stay local; the continuation key is codex:home:<sharedHomePath>. Threads can continue across instances that share a continuation key.
verevonRelevance: A direct model for Verevon's BYOK and subscription routes: separate credentials per instance but a shared continuation identity so a conversation can move between equivalent accounts.
notes: The overlay needs symlinks, which are privileged on Windows without developer mode; the code reports a typed error when a shadow entry cannot be linked.

name: ProviderService facade: thread-bound routing, lazy session recovery and stale-session cleanup
what: One service routes every session and turn call to the right adapter. If a session is not live (for example after a restart), it is recovered from a persisted binding and resume cursor on first use.
how: ProviderSessionDirectory persists a binding per thread {provider, providerInstanceId, adapterKey, status, resumeCursor, runtimePayload (cwd, modelSelection), runtimeMode}. resolveRoutableSession finds the binding, asks the adapter hasSession, and when absent and recovery is allowed calls recoverSessionForThread: it requires a stored resume cursor, re-prepares the MCP credential, calls adapter.startSession with the persisted cwd, model and runtime mode, verifies the adapter/provider match and re-binds. stopStaleSessionsForThread stops the same thread on other adapters when the user switches instance. Inputs are decoded with Schema and mapped to validation errors; all calls emit metrics and analytics events; a single PubSub fans out canonical runtime events and logs them to the canonical NDJSON stream.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's session-core already owns durable run state; persisting a provider resume cursor per thread and recovering lazily on the next turn is a cheap way to survive gateway restarts for long agent sessions.
notes: A single in-process PubSub with no backpressure design is fine for one user and would need a bounded, tenant-partitioned bus (NATS) in Verevon.

name: Idle session reaper that respects active turns and native background work
what: Provider processes that have been idle for 30 minutes are stopped to free resources, unless a turn is running or the agent still has background tasks (subagents, workflows, monitors).
how: ProviderSessionReaper sweeps every 5 minutes over persisted bindings not already stopped, parses lastSeenAt, skips sessions whose thread shell has an active turn id or a non-null backgroundLiveness, and otherwise calls providerService.stopSession (logging reason inactivity_threshold). ThreadBackgroundLivenessService keeps an in-memory per-thread registry of live agent and monitor tasks fed by task lifecycle events, reporting 'working' or 'monitoring'; it is deliberately not persisted because orphaned background work is not live after a restart.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's sandbox leases and background processes (S4.2) need the same rule: never reap an idle session that still owns a running subagent, process or watch; derive liveness from task events instead of timers.
notes: The reaper makes a stopped session cheap to resume because of the lazy recovery record above.

name: Claude Agent SDK driven in streaming-input mode against the user's own Claude Code binary
what: T3 does not call the Anthropic API for coding turns. It runs the user's installed Claude Code through the Agent SDK and feeds messages into a live session, so model, effort and permission mode can change mid-session and a message sent while a turn runs steers it.
how: startSession builds ClaudeQueryOptions with pathToClaudeCodeExecutable (the configured binary), systemPrompt preset 'claude_code', settingSources user/project/local (so the user's Claude settings, memory files and skills apply), includePartialMessages true, permissionMode from the runtime mode (auto-accept-edits gives acceptEdits, auto gives auto, full-access gives bypassPermissions with allowDangerouslySkipPermissions), a settings overlay (alwaysThinkingEnabled, fastMode, ultracode, autoCompactWindow), additionalDirectories [cwd, attachments dir], env with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, extraArgs from launchArgs, and an http mcpServers entry 't3-code' with a bearer header. The prompt is an AsyncIterable fed from an Effect Queue (Stream.toAsyncIterable), canUseTool and onUserDialog callbacks bridge approvals and questions into the event pipeline, and sendTurn calls query.setModel when the model changed and query.setPermissionMode('plan' or the session's base mode) for the interaction mode before offering the next message; a message sent while a turn is active reuses the running turn (steering).
verevonRelevance: Verevon calls hosted models directly, but the streaming-input design (a long-lived session fed by a queue, with callbacks for permission and user dialogs) is the right shape for its Do-mode loop if it ever mid-run steers or switches model/effort.
notes: Requires the user's own Claude Code install and login; the adapter file is the largest in the server (161 KB).

name: Claude interrupt is a hard session stop; rewind trims adapter bookkeeping only
what: Pressing stop on a Claude thread closes the SDK query and escalates to SIGKILL if needed, then the next message resumes from the saved cursor. Reverting to an earlier turn restores files, but the Claude-side conversation rollback is lighter than Codex's.
how: interruptTurn calls stopSessionInternal (comment: interrupt() can acknowledge while resumed background tasks keep the CLI alive, so stop is a hard boundary). The resume cursor is {threadId, resume (session UUID), resumeSessionAt (last assistant message UUID), turnCount}; lastAssistantUuid is set when assistant messages arrive. rollbackThread only splices the adapter's in-memory turn list and refreshes the cursor, without changing resumeSessionAt, whereas Codex implements rollbackThread through the real thread/rollback request.
verevonRelevance: When Verevon adds rewind (currently absent) it should make provider conversation rollback explicit and per-provider, not assume file revert implies model context revert.
notes: INF (medium): because resumeSessionAt is not moved back on rollback, a resumed Claude session may still carry later turns in model context after a checkpoint revert; this was not verified at runtime.

name: Codex app-server per-thread process with generated client and runtime-mode mapping
what: Each Codex thread gets its own `codex app-server` child speaking JSON-RPC over stdio. T3's four runtime modes translate to Codex's approval policy, sandbox and approvals reviewer, and revert uses Codex's native thread rollback.
how: CodexSessionRuntime spawns the configured binary with args [app-server, ...launchArgs] (T3CODE_CODEX_LAUNCH_ARGS overrides), cwd per thread, CODEX_HOME from the instance and forceKillAfter 2 s; then initialize + initialized, then openCodexThread (thread/start or thread/resume with recoverable-error snippets such as 'no such thread'). runtimeModeToThreadConfig maps approval-required to untrusted + read-only + reviewer user, auto-accept-edits to on-request + workspace-write, auto to on-request + workspace-write + approvals reviewer auto_review, and full-access to never + danger-full-access; the reviewer is always sent so a mode switch cannot leave auto_review sticky. Approvals, user input and MCP elicitation arrive as server requests held in pending maps. Child agents are registered from explicit thread_spawn signals and re-emitted as synthetic collabAgent events.
verevonRelevance: Directly comparable to Verevon's Integration Core Codex app-server route; the runtime-mode table and the 'always send the reviewer' lesson apply to any permission mapping.
notes: The auto mode relies on Codex's AI reviewer; providers without one fall back to supervised behavior (see the OpenCode record).

name: ACP adapters for Cursor and Grok with minimal client capabilities and vendor extensions
what: Cursor's `cursor-agent` and Grok's `grok agent stdio` are driven through the open Agent Client Protocol. T3 offers no filesystem or terminal tools to them, only permission and elicitation handling plus vendor extension methods for questions, plans and todos.
how: AcpSessionRuntime initializes with clientCapabilities fs.readTextFile/writeTextFile false and terminal false (agent runs its own tools), authenticates, then loads, resumes or creates the session; session/load races the RPC response against a replay idle gap under a timeout while a load gate holds back replayed history notifications. Mode aliases map plan (plan, architect), implement (code, agent, default, chat, implement) and approval (ask) to T3's interaction modes. Cursor extension schemas (ask_question, create_plan, update_todos) and a Grok/xAI extension are decoded to T3's user-input and plan events; in full-access mode permission requests are auto-approved by selecting an allow option.
verevonRelevance: Verevon documents no ACP/AG-UI support; implementing an ACP client in Rust would let it host Cursor, Grok, Gemini CLI and Claude-compatible agents as selectable runtimes behind the same governance pipeline.
notes: Vendor extensions are the fragile part: they track undocumented-or-private method schemas (a Cursor extension reference is cited in a source comment).

name: OpenCode adapter: spawned `opencode serve`, SDK client and a runtime-mode permission ruleset
what: OpenCode is driven over its local HTTP server using its SDK. T3 either spawns the server for the session or attaches to a user-configured URL with Basic auth.
how: opencodeRuntime spawns `opencode serve --hostname --port` and waits for the 'opencode server listening' line (30 s), or uses serverUrl without owning its lifetime; createOpencodeClient talks to it (optional Basic header with serverPassword) and event.subscribe streams events (logged as opencode.sdk.event). buildOpenCodePermissionRules maps full-access to allow-all and other modes to an ask-by-default ruleset (bash, webfetch, websearch, codesearch, external_directory, doom_loop ask; edit allow only for auto-accept-edits; question allow). Rollback uses session.revert. Skill discovery output is capped at 8 MiB.
verevonRelevance: Shows how an HTTP-native agent runtime is wrapped behind the same adapter contract; the explicit permission ruleset per mode is a good table to mirror in Verevon's capability policy.
notes: OpenCode can use local or custom models, so this is also T3's only path to non-vendor models (INF low; not verified).

name: Canonical provider runtime event taxonomy that preserves the raw native payload
what: Five protocols (Claude SDK messages, Codex app-server notifications, ACP JSON-RPC, OpenCode SDK events, plus extensions) are normalized into one stream of 48 event types, 16 item types and 10 request types, with the original payload attached for debugging.
how: providerRuntime.ts defines RuntimeEventRaw {source (codex.app-server.notification|request, codex.eventmsg, claude.sdk.message|permission, codex.sdk.thread-event, opencode.sdk.event, acp.jsonrpc, acp.<vendor>.extension), method, messageType, payload}, the 48 ProviderRuntimeEventType literals (session.*, thread.*, turn.*, item.*, content.delta, request.*, user-input.*, task.*, hook.*, tool.*, auth/account/mcp, model.rerouted, config/deprecation warnings, files.persisted, runtime.warning/error), TOOL_LIFECYCLE_ITEM_TYPES (command_execution, file_change, mcp_tool_call, dynamic_tool_call, collab_agent_tool_call, web_search, image_view), content stream kinds (assistant_text, reasoning_text, reasoning_summary_text, plan_text, command_output, file_change_output) and request types (command/file read/file change/apply patch/exec approvals, MCP elicitation, tool user input, dynamic tool call, token refresh). ProviderService logs this canonical stream beside the native stream.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's typed SSE events are Model Plane specific; defining a canonical event schema that other runtimes (ACP, Codex) can be mapped onto is the prerequisite for hosting them, and the raw-payload attachment makes mapping bugs diagnosable.
notes: The sibling UI audit counted the same taxonomy (its record 056); the counts here (48/16/10) were re-derived from the source. Event 'thread.realtime.*' events mirror Codex realtime but no T3 audio pipeline exists.

name: Lifecycle guard that rejects stale or out-of-order provider events
what: A late completion from an old turn, or a resume handshake that looks like a turn, cannot overwrite the thread's real running state.
how: ProviderRuntimeIngestion applies thread-lifecycle events through shouldApplyThreadLifecycle when STRICT_PROVIDER_LIFECYCLE_GUARD is on (default; disabled only by T3CODE_STRICT_PROVIDER_LIFECYCLE_GUARD=0): turn.started is ignored if it conflicts with an active turn unless a turn start is pending; turn.completed must name the active turn, and an untargeted completion is dropped (the known emitter was the Claude resume handshake, system/init plus result(num_turns:0)); runtime.error only applies to the active turn or when none is tracked. Ingestion caches (10k turn-message ids, 20k buffered texts, 120 min TTL) are bounded.
verevonRelevance: Any multi-protocol ingestion layer needs this guard; Verevon can express it as a state-machine check in session-core when merging events from Do-mode workers, subagents and replays.
notes: Evidence that provider protocols leak lifecycle ambiguities that a canonical layer must police.

name: Assistant text is buffered server-side and flushed as one message; token streaming is a legacy mode
what: By default the timeline updates when a message is complete (or at a size cap) rather than on every token, which keeps the event log small. A legacy setting restores token-level streaming.
how: ProviderRuntimeIngestion accumulates assistant deltas in a TTL cache keyed by message id (cap MAX_BUFFERED_ASSISTANT_CHARS 24,000, then a safety valve flushes the buffer as a delta), flushes buffered messages at turn end or item completion (flushBufferedAssistantMessage), and does the same for proposed-plan text. The setting enableLegacyTokenStreaming switches to per-delta commands (thread.message.assistant.delta).
verevonRelevance: Verevon streams typed SSE tokens; the useful trick is to keep token deltas out of the durable log and persist only completed messages, while a separate ephemeral channel carries partials.
notes: Trade-off: the UI loses perceived responsiveness versus peers (claude.ai, ChatGPT) that stream tokens; the sibling audit lists this under weaknesses.

name: Workspace checkpoints as hidden git refs captured through a temporary index; revert coordinates files, provider and refs
what: Before and after each turn T3 snapshots the working tree (including untracked files) without touching the user's index or branches. Reverting restores files, rolls the provider conversation back, deletes newer snapshots and refreshes the file picker.
how: GitVcsDriver.captureCheckpoint uses a temporary GIT_INDEX_FILE inside the git common dir: read-tree HEAD, add -A, write-tree, commit-tree (author 'T3 Code') and update-ref to refs/t3/checkpoints/<base64url(threadId)>/turn/<n>; restoreCheckpoint runs git restore --source <commit> --worktree --staged then git clean -fd and git reset; diffCheckpoints compares refs with an ignore-whitespace option. CheckpointReactor captures a pre-turn baseline (turn 0) and per-turn checkpoints, and on thread.checkpoint-revert-requested validates the git workspace and turn count, restores, refreshes workspace entries, calls providerService.rollbackConversation for the number of rolled-back turns, deletes stale refs and dispatches thread.revert.complete; failures are recorded as checkpoint.revert.failed activities.
verevonRelevance: Verevon has no rewind; for sandbox workspaces a content-addressed snapshot per run (Verevon already has CAS-backed workspace manifests) plus a coordinated provider/conversation rollback would deliver the same user-facing feature.
notes: Correction to the scout: CheckpointStore itself does not coordinate provider rollback, but CheckpointReactor does (providerService.rollbackConversation). git clean -fd does not remove ignored files; checkpoints require a git repository. Whether the model context truly rewinds depends on the provider (see the Claude rollback record).

name: Worktree-per-thread lifecycle with managed paths, submodule init, base-branch metadata and self-healing
what: A thread can run in its own git worktree under the app's base directory. If the folder disappears it is recreated from the branch on the next turn, and the branch is renamed after the first message using an AI-generated name.
how: createWorktree builds <baseDir>/worktrees/<repoName>/<sanitized-branch> with git worktree add (-b newRef baseRef), runs submodule update --init --recursive best-effort, and stores branch.<name>.gh-merge-base. ProviderCommandReactor.ensureThreadWorktree checks the persisted path, prunes stale admin entries and recreates it before every turn; on the first message it forks title generation and worktree-branch rename tasks. The turn-start bootstrap can fetch origin, resolve a remote tracking commit and base the worktree on it when 'start from origin' is enabled and an origin remote exists. ReviewService only reads diffs for cwds inside the workspace root or the worktrees root (canonicalized).
verevonRelevance: Verevon is not an IDE and its ledger rejected worktree isolation for subagents, but for any code-capable Do mode the 'recreate missing workspace before each turn' rule and path-containment check are worth copying.
notes: Worktrees live outside the repo, so the user's repo stays clean; checkpoints work per worktree.

name: Single-command bootstrap saga: create thread, prepare worktree, run setup script, start turn, roll back on failure
what: The first message of a new thread is one atomic server-side workflow, so the client does not orchestrate several round trips or leave half-created threads behind.
how: dispatchBootstrapTurnStart in ws.ts runs a bootstrapProgram: optional thread.create dispatch, then prepareWorktree (fetch origin, resolve base commit, createWorktree with newRefName and baseRefName, thread.meta.update with branch and path, refresh git status), then the project setup script runner (t3.json runOnWorktreeCreate) with launch/failure activities, then the final thread.turn.start command. On failure, cleanupCreatedThread runs uninterruptibly and the error carries bootstrapThreadDisposition 'deleted'. All of it is enqueued behind the command-readiness gate.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's 'start a run in a Space' path (lease, workspace hydrate, plan, run) could be a single saga command with compensation, which also gives clean error semantics to the SPA.
notes: The saga is imperative code inside the WebSocket handler (ws.ts is 108 KB), not a reusable workflow engine.

name: Context compaction and resume prompts for long Claude sessions
what: Compaction boundaries from the SDK show up as timeline events, an auto-compact window can be set, and when resuming a very old, large session the SDK's own question 'compact it first?' is surfaced as a normal user-input request with a never-ask-again answer.
how: ClaudeAdapter maps the SDK system/compact_boundary message to a token-usage snapshot (thread.token-usage.updated) plus a thread.state.changed event with state 'compacted', and applies settings.autoCompactWindow from the provider settings. It declares supportedDialogKinds ['resume_return'] and implements onUserDialog (handleResumeDialog), which builds the question text from session age and estimated tokens and offers three answers (Compact and continue, Keep full history, Don't ask again) (shared claudeCompaction.ts also exports the matching pattern so the web client can recognize it and mirror the 'Don't ask again' dismissal in localStorage).
verevonRelevance: Verevon compacts silently in the gateway; exposing an explicit 'resume a stale, large session: compact?' decision to the user (with a remembered default) is a transparent alternative for long-lived threads.
notes: Manual compaction is Claude-only (sibling audit: it injects /compact).

name: Subagent, task and workflow mapping from provider streams to timeline rows
what: Claude subagents, background shells, workflows and Codex child agents all surface as task.* events with identity (role, model, effort, title, owning agent), so the UI can show fleets and the server can compute background liveness.
how: ClaudeAdapter remembers per-task identity from task_started (taskId, toolUseId, subagent type, task type, workflow name, owning agent via the launching tool, model and effort inherited from the Agent tool input or session), repeats a linkage bundle on every later task.* payload, bounds workflow phases and agents (64/100), dedupes workflow member arrays by fingerprint (task_progress repeats the full array each tick) and suppresses subagent narration deltas. CodexSessionRuntime registers children from thread_spawn signals and re-emits them as synthetic collabAgent events marked timelineBypass; the spawn turn id lets the UI group fleets. ThreadPlanProgress and ThreadBackgroundLiveness consume the same stream.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's subagents are depth-1 child runs; self-describing task events (identity repeated on every progress row so it survives log retention) is a cheap improvement for its run/child-run timeline.
notes: Codex child-agent registration is marked WIP and probe-gated in a source comment.

name: Utility-model calls through one-shot CLI structured output, with first-turn title and branch generation
what: Commit messages, PR titles/bodies, thread titles and branch names are written by a chosen model by invoking the same agent CLIs in non-interactive mode with a JSON schema, not by calling provider APIs.
how: ClaudeTextGeneration spawns `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema <schema>` (180 s timeout) and decodes structured_output; CodexTextGeneration spawns `codex exec --ephemeral --skip-git-repo-check --output-schema`; Cursor, Grok and OpenCode have their own implementations behind the same TextGeneration service held by each ProviderInstance. Prompts and presets live in TextGenerationPrompts/Presets; schemas come from Effect Schema converted to JSON Schema. ProviderCommandReactor triggers title and worktree-branch generation on the first user message in forked fibers.
verevonRelevance: Verevon routes cheap utility calls through its intent router; T3's split (utility model selected separately from the main model, schema-validated output) matches that and could back titles, summaries and commit-style outputs.
notes: Spawning a CLI per utility call is slower than an API call but reuses the user's existing auth with zero extra credentials.

name: Approval and user-input requests are provider-held callbacks that become stale after restart
what: Approval prompts live inside the provider process. If the app or session restarts, a pending approval cannot be answered anymore, and T3 says so explicitly instead of failing silently.
how: Claude holds approvals in pendingApprovals/pendingUserInputs Deferreds resolved by canUseTool and AskUserQuestion; Codex holds them in pending maps keyed by request id. ProviderCommandReactor builds the message 'Stale pending <kind> request ... callback state does not survive app restarts or recovered sessions. Restart the turn to continue.' when a response targets a request the live session no longer has, and records it as a failed approval-response activity. A pendingApprovals projector tracks open requests for the sidebar and for the notification relay.
verevonRelevance: Verevon persists approvals durably with encrypted continuation descriptors, which is strictly better; the lesson is the explicit 'stale request' error path for any approval whose backing run no longer exists.
notes: This is a limitation of driving external agent processes; the loop cannot be resumed after approval if the process is gone.

name: Provider snapshot lifecycle: instant initial snapshot, probe, progressive enrichment and disk status cache
what: The model picker and provider health appear immediately from a cached or static snapshot and are refined by background probes, so a slow CLI never blocks the UI.
how: makeManagedServerProvider takes getSettings/streamSettings, initialSnapshot, checkProvider and an optional enrichSnapshot that can publish additional snapshots with a generation counter; a refresh semaphore serializes probes, refresh respects BackgroundPolicy demand and providerHealthRefreshInterval, and a PubSub streams changes to subscribed clients. providerStatusCache persists snapshots per instance under <base>/caches and hydrateCachedProvider merges cached models into the fallback snapshot only when instance id and driver match. Probes have a 4 s default timeout.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's model picker could render from a cached capability snapshot and refine asynchronously instead of waiting for provider probes in the request path.
notes: The enrichment-generation counter prevents a slow older probe from overwriting a newer snapshot.

name: Provider CLI maintenance: version advisories and one-click install commands
what: The app notices when an agent CLI has a newer version and can run the right installer (npm, pnpm, bun, brew) for the way it was installed, serialized by a lock.
how: providerMaintenance caches the latest published version (1 h TTL, 4 s timeout) from the package registry, computes a ServerProviderVersionAdvisory, and exposes ProviderMaintenanceCapabilities {packageName, update action {command, executable, args, lockKey}}; providerMaintenanceRunner/CommandCoordinator execute updates and stream status; server.updateProvider is the RPC. Dismissed notification keys and update checks are settings.
verevonRelevance: Not applicable to hosted inference; relevant only to a future local-runtime companion.
notes: Marked medium confidence because only the head of the runner and coordinator files was read.

name: Attachments: signed upload URLs, files on disk, path injected into the turn and a scoped directory grant
what: Pasted images are uploaded over HTTP, stored by id under the state directory, and given to the agent both as pixels and as a file path the agent may read without an approval prompt.
how: attachments.createUploadUrl returns an upload URL for /api/attachments/upload; files land in <state>/attachments (pending attachments are swept at startup). ProviderService appends '[Attached image "name" is saved at: <path>]' lines to the turn input, adapters inline the image content into the model prompt, and the Claude adapter grants the attachments directory as an additional directory so the agent can read or copy it without approval while secrets and the database stay outside the grant. Workspace images and HTML previews are served through short-lived HMAC-signed /api/assets URLs.
verevonRelevance: Pattern for Verevon's file-in-chat path: store once, reference by id, and make the capability to read it explicit (a scoped grant) rather than implicit filesystem access.
notes: Only images are first-class in the composer (sibling audit); no audio/video/document generation exists.

name: WSL as a second concurrent backend with its own home, database and preflight
what: On Windows the user can run an additional backend inside a WSL distro, side by side with the Windows one, or WSL-only. The two have separate state and both appear as environments in the sidebar.
how: resolveWslStartConfig launches `wsl.exe [-d distro] --exec env PATH=... <resolved node> <linux entry> --bootstrap-fd 0` with the bootstrap envelope on stdin (wsl.exe drops extra fds). A preflight resolves node and the user PATH through a login shell, converts the entry path with wslpath and classifies failures as transient (retry limit) or fatal. The packaged server.asar is materialized into a version-marked directory (t3code-wsl-server-tree.json) because plain node cannot read an asar. The WSL server binds 0.0.0.0 so the Windows side can reach it through localhost forwarding or the distro IP, omits t3Home so it uses its own Linux home and SQLite file (T3CODE_HOME is stripped to avoid both backends sharing a /mnt/c database), forwards selected env through WSLENV, and reports resource telemetry as unavailable (the sidecar is a Windows exe). The renderer registers it as a desktop-local environment, minting a bearer via the bootstrap token.
verevonRelevance: None for hosted chat; it is a useful reference for running a Linux toolchain next to a Windows UI, which Verevon solves with Linux sandboxes instead.
notes: Not comparable in any other desktop app audited. Heavy platform-specific code (wsl.exe quirks) for one OS combination.

name: SSH remote environments via scripted remote launch, reused server, loopback tunnel and in-app password prompt
what: A user can point the app at an SSH host. T3 installs or reuses a T3 server there, keeps it running, forwards a local port to it and pairs automatically, so the agents run on the remote machine while the UI stays local.
how:
launchOrReuseRemoteServer sends a shell script over ssh stdin that resolves the t3 CLI (npx --yes or npm exec of an exact package spec derived from the app version and update channel; it verifies that the CLI actually exists after install, with a hint about node-pty native builds), keeps state in ~/.t3/ssh-launch/, reuses a running server (server-runtime.json) or starts `nohup env T3CODE_NO_BROWSER=1 t3 serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port

--base-dir ...`, and prints {remotePort, serverKind}. issueRemotePairingToken mints a token over SSH; startSshTunnel runs ssh -N -L :127.0.0.1: with ExitOnForwardFailure, ControlMaster=no, ServerAliveInterval=15 and CountMax=3. Passwords never appear in argv: the renderer shows an in-app prompt, and ssh is re-run with SSH_ASKPASS/SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force pointing at generated POSIX and Windows helper scripts that read the cached value. Hosts are discovered from the user's ssh config.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's remote execution is its own sandbox fleet, but the pattern of a pinned-version remote bootstrap with reuse, plus pairing, is the template for any customer-hosted worker (on-prem runner) agent.
notes: Relies on the remote host having node/npm and a C toolchain for node-pty; failure messages are specific. The remote server is a full T3 server (not a thin agent), so remote auth uses the same pairing system.

name: Thread-scoped PTY terminals with persisted history, subprocess detection and Bun/Node adapters
what: Each thread can have several terminals that survive reconnects, keep a scrollback on disk, show which command is running, and can be used as agent context.
how: TerminalManager holds sessions keyed by (threadId, terminalId) over a PtyAdapter chosen at runtime (BunPtyAdapter or NodePtyAdapter with node-pty, ConPTY on Windows). Output is fanned out as attach/subscribe streams (subscribeTerminalEvents, subscribeTerminalMetadata); history is persisted per thread/terminal to <logs>/terminals/*.log with a 5,000-line limit and 40 ms debounce; up to 128 inactive sessions are retained; a poller (1 s) inspects the process tree (ps on POSIX, Get-CimInstance Win32_Process on Windows) to flag hasRunningSubprocess and a normalized child command label; spawn env strips PORT, ELECTRON_RENDERER_PORT, ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE and AppImage runtime variables; kill uses a 1 s grace. The RPC methods are open, attach, write, resize, clear, restart and close under a dedicated terminal scope.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's `process_*` tools under bwrap could expose the same 'is a command still running, and which one' signal and persisted scrollback to the Do-mode UI.
notes: Terminal output as composer context chips is a UI feature covered by the sibling audit. The terminal scope is separate from orchestration scope, which allows a read-only client without shell access.

name: Agent-driven embedded browser: CDP debugger, injected Playwright runtime and native input events
what: Agents can open, inspect and operate a page inside the app's own preview browser. Locators work like Playwright's (roles, text, test ids) without launching a Playwright browser.
how: The preview runs in Electron webviews on persistent partitions. A single control session per webContents (a Semaphore) attaches wc.debugger (CDP 1.3); it refuses if DevTools is open or another debugger is attached. ensurePlaywrightInjected extracts Playwright's InjectedScript source from playwright-core's lib/coreBundle.js by marker/terminator, evaluates it in a VM with a 1 s timeout and a 100 KB minimum-length check, and installs globalThis.__t3PlaywrightInjected with testIdAttributeName data-testid. Click resolves a locator via injected.parseSelector/querySelector, checks visible and enabled state, scrolls into view and computes the center point; before clicking it emits agent-cursor pointer events (move, then click) to the UI so the user sees where the agent acts, checks the point is inside the viewport, then sends CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent mousePressed/mouseReleased; typing edits through the injected page runtime (a source comment notes CDP Input.insertText drops text until a hidden guest is activated) and key presses use Input.dispatchKeyEvent. Snapshots return URL, title, loading state, visible text, interactive elements, an accessibility tree, console and network entries, an action timeline and a PNG screenshot. Emulated color scheme is applied through CDP Emulation.setEmulatedMedia.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's rule is 'Model proposes, Quarry executes'; T3's perception design (accessibility tree plus console/network/action timeline plus screenshot in one snapshot, and locator-based actions) is a concrete richer observation schema Quarry could return to the model.
notes: Scraping the Playwright bundle by string marker (source3 = ...) is brittle across playwright-core versions (the code validates length and fails with typed errors). Everything runs on the user's desktop, not in a sandbox.

name: Browser-host broker: agent on any server drives a browser on the user's desktop through a reverse RPC with session-to-host leases
what: The agent may run on a remote machine while the browser it controls is the one open on the user's own desktop. The server relays each tool call to the right desktop client and pins the session to that client so multi-step flows keep cookies and DOM state.
how: Desktop clients call previewAutomation.connect (a server-to-client stream of requests) advertising their environment id, supported operations and focus order, answer with previewAutomation.respond, and report focus with previewAutomation.focusHost. PreviewAutomationBroker keeps clients, per-session HostAssignment leases and pending requests in a SynchronizedRef. invoke() picks the leased host if it is live and supports the operation, otherwise the best host by number of supported operations, then focus, then recency; a live lease is never silently moved to a newer client (the caller gets a capability error and may start a new provider session); a dead lease is pruned and may fail over. Timeouts, oversize results (64 KB for evaluate), selector errors and disconnects map to typed errors.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's browser grants and Quarry live frames could use the same lease idea to bind a Do-mode run to one browser session/host, and the reverse-RPC pattern to let a cloud run drive a user-owned browser when a grant exists.
notes: The REA/IPC listing shows the desktop side as desktop:preview-automation-* channels. The 64 KB evaluate cap is from a tool description string; the typed ResultTooLarge error is in Manager.ts:3573.

name: Preview recording and screenshots built on CDP screencast frames and renderer-side encoding
what: A browser tab can be recorded to MP4 or WebM and saved as an artifact, and screenshots can be copied or revealed, all from the same preview.
how: startFrameCapture subscribes consumers (recording, screenshots) to CDP Page.startScreencast; Page.screencastFrame events are acked and, when a recording consumer exists, delivered to the renderer as DesktopPreviewRecordingFrame {tabId, data, width, height, receivedAt}; the renderer encodes with MediaRecorder (MP4/H.264 when supported, else WebM) and sends bytes back through desktop:preview-recording-save, where the manager writes browser-recording-<id>.<ext> into the artifact directory and returns an artifact record. Screenshots use webContents.capturePage; background throttling is disabled while capturing. The same operations are exposed to agents as preview_recording_start/stop.
verevonRelevance: Recorded agent browser sessions are a strong transparency artifact; Verevon's Quarry could store screencast artifacts per run next to its Proof Bundle.
notes: Encoding in the renderer ties recording quality to the UI process.
