name: Local dev-server discovery with bounded HTML probing and reference-counted polling
what: The app notices web servers the agent started (dev servers on localhost) and offers them in the preview, without showing every listening port.
how: PortScanner lists listeners with `lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -P -n -F pcn` on macOS/Linux, with PowerShell Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen on Windows (fallback: a curated list of common dev ports), then publishes a port only after a bounded HTTP(S) probe finds an HTML document or a redirect to one; positive and negative results are cached briefly by URL and listener identity. Polling is reference counted by scoped retain, so the single fiber is a no-op with zero subscribers. Configured URLs from t3.json previewUrl are included.
verevonRelevance: Low for chat; relevant if Verevon adds a code-capable mode with live previews of agent-built apps.
notes: Corrects the scout: the Windows branch exists (PowerShell Get-NetTCPConnection).

name: VCS driver SPI with a git implementation, detection cache and demand-driven status broadcaster
what: All repository operations go through a driver interface with declared capabilities, so another VCS can be added. Status is computed once per directory and shared with every subscribed client.
how: VcsDriver exposes capabilities, execute, optional checkpoints and getDiffPreview, detectRepository, isInsideWorkTree, listWorkspaceFiles, listRemotes, filterIgnoredPaths and initRepository; VcsDriverRegistry detects the driver per cwd with a cache (no caching of misses) and has only 'git' registered, although VcsDriverKind already includes 'jj' and source-control discovery has Jujutsu install hints. VcsStatusBroadcaster refreshes shared status every 30 s with failure backoff up to 15 minutes and streams subscribeVcsStatus results with freshness labels (live-local, cached-local, cached-remote, explicit-remote). GitVcsDriverCore (117 KB) wraps process execution with timeouts.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's Data v2 and Ingestion planes already abstract providers; the 'capabilities record on the driver plus optional operations' shape is a good way to model provider actions with uneven support.
notes: Only git is implemented; jj is anticipated, not shipped.

name: Four source-control hosts behind one registry using the user's installed CLIs, with rate-limit cooldown
what: Pull requests, reviews, checks and comments work on GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps and Bitbucket through the user's own gh, glab and az logins (Bitbucket via API token), without T3 holding forge credentials.
how: SourceControlProviderRegistry and PullRequestProviderRegistry map a host to a provider implementation (GitHubCli/GitHubPullRequestCli with a GraphQL budget guard, GitLabCli, AzureDevOpsCli, BitbucketApi). Auth status helpers check gh/glab login; Bitbucket reads T3CODE_BITBUCKET_EMAIL/API_TOKEN/ACCESS_TOKEN. SourceControlRateLimit tracks per provider/host cooldowns (30 s base, up to 15 min). One PullRequestService instance backs both WebSocket and HTTP APIs, so caches single-flight across clients and WebSocket mutations invalidate data later read over HTTP. Text generation can write commit and PR text with a selected model and the repo's PR template.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's integration-corev2 provider actions could reuse the 'reuse the user's tool login, share a cache, cool down on rate limit' approach for forge actions.
notes: Coding-specific; Verevon is not an IDE, so only the harness patterns matter.

name: Per-session scoped MCP server exposed to every agent through its native config mechanism
what: T3 hosts one MCP endpoint (/mcp) that gives agents browser tools. Each provider session gets its own short-lived bearer credential limited to specific capabilities, and every adapter injects it in the way its protocol supports.
how: McpSessionRegistry.issue creates a 32-byte random token, stores only its SHA-256 hash with a scope {environmentId, threadId, providerSessionId, providerInstanceId, capabilities Set(['preview']), issuedAt}, and prunes records after a 24 h liveness window refreshed by every provider turn (touch) and MCP call; stopSession/stopAll revoke eagerly. ProviderService.prepareMcpSession fails closed: if the enableAgentBrowserAccess setting is off or unreadable it revokes the credential and clears the session config. Injection: Claude SDK mcpServers {'t3-code': {type: http, url, Authorization header}}; Codex `-c mcp_servers.t3-code.url=...` plus bearer_token_env_var=T3_MCP_BEARER_TOKEN (token via env, not argv); ACP agents via the session/new mcpServers array; OpenCode via the SDK call mcp.add {name t3-code, type remote, url, Authorization header, oauth false}, only for an OpenCode server that T3 spawned itself (not for a user-configured external server). McpHttpServer is an Effect McpServer with an auth middleware (401 + WWW-Authenticate Bearer on bad credentials, logged reason) and normalizes empty 200 bodies to 202.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's baseline says MCP tools cannot be invoked by either loop; T3 shows a concrete way to expose platform tools to runtimes: per-run capability-scoped credentials, hashed at rest, fail-closed gating and one endpoint that every runtime can reach.
notes: /mcp is mounted outside the environment auth stack and is reachable on whatever host the server binds to (a source comment says the token is the only guard on a remote-reachable server). Only one toolkit (preview) exists, so this is a mechanism with a single use. Credentials live in a module-global map, so they do not survive a restart.

name: Preview MCP toolkit with honest tool annotations and a mixed-version operation set
what: Fourteen browser tools are defined once as typed Effect tools and published over MCP with readOnly, destructive, idempotent and open-world hints that match what each tool does.
how: tools.ts defines helpers browserTool (openWorld, destructive), safeBrowserTool (not destructive) and readonlyBrowserTool (readOnly and idempotent) and applies them to preview_open, navigate, status, snapshot, click, type, press, scroll, wait_for, evaluate, resize, set_appearance and recording start/stop with long descriptions that steer the model (prefer a Playwright locator, call snapshot before acting, 64 KB evaluate cap). handlers.ts maps each to a broker operation; open input normalizes the show alias to open and leaves the user's auto-show preference alone. The snapshot tool is registered separately so its result can return the PNG as an MCP image content block; failures become isError CallToolResults without leaking details. PREVIEW_AUTOMATION_V1_OPERATIONS vs the current list lets old desktops keep working.
verevonRelevance: A template for how Verevon should describe its own tools to models and to MCP clients: accurate hint annotations, steering descriptions and a snapshot-before-act contract.
notes: The tool list matches the scout's count of 14 names.

name: CLI front door that acts as a client of a live server and falls back to an offline engine
what: Commands such as `t3 project add|remove|rename` work whether or not the server is running: when it is, they go through its API; when it is not, they run the same engine against the database directly.
how: The server persists server-runtime.json (version, pid, host, port, origin, devUrl, startedAt) atomically while listening and clears it on shutdown. The CLI's tryResolveLiveProjectExecutionMode reads it, issues an administrative-scope session (label 't3 project cli') straight from the shared SQLite-backed EnvironmentAuth for the duration of the command (acquireUseRelease revokes it afterwards), fetches /api/orchestration/snapshot and dispatches via /api/orchestration/dispatch; if the probe fails it clears the stale state and builds an offline runtime layer (OrchestrationEngine over the same state.sqlite, which is why busy_timeout is set). Other commands: start, serve, service install/update/uninstall/status, pair, auth (pairing and session issue/list/revoke), connect (login, link, publish, unlink), config, triage. detectCliRunner recognizes npx/pnpm dlx/bunx launches so suggested commands are copy-pasteable, and nightly builds keep the @nightly tag.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's ops tooling could follow the same rule for admin CLIs: talk to the running service when reachable, never write behind its back, and have a clearly labelled offline mode.
notes: The CLI can mint administrative sessions because it shares the state directory and signing key with the server, so filesystem access to the state directory equals admin access; that is intentional for a single-user machine and would be unacceptable in a multi-tenant service.

name: `t3 triage`: hand a misbehaving install to a local coding agent with machine facts and a remote playbook
what: A support command collects version, paths and server liveness into context.md and launches the user's own Claude or Codex with a built-in playbook to diagnose the install, asking before writing to the database.
how: cli/triage.ts writes the context file and launches `claude` or `codex` interactively (agent and model are flags). triagePrompt.ts holds the playbook text, which tells the agent to fetch the current .github/triage/PLAYBOOK.md from the main branch and fall back to the bundled copy.
verevonRelevance: A neat support pattern (self-service diagnosis by an agent with scoped context); but a remote playbook fetched from a branch is a prompt-injection and supply-chain surface that Verevon should avoid or pin by digest.
notes: The playbook was not fetched during this audit. The trust boundary (remote text steering a coding agent) was already noted by the scout.

name: Project config file t3.json and setup scripts that run in a terminal on worktree creation
what: A repository can carry t3.json to define scripts (with keybindings), a preview URL, auto-open behavior, a default thread environment mode and an icon; a setup script runs when a worktree is created.
how: T3ProjectFileLoader best-effort loads and validates the checked-in file (missing or invalid means absent); the schema is published at t3.codes/schema/t3.json; ProjectSetupScriptRunner.runForThread starts the configured script in a thread terminal inside the worktree and reports started/failed as activities; shared projectScripts helpers drive keybindings.
verevonRelevance: Equivalent of repo-level agent configuration; for Verevon the analogue is Space-level instructions and scripts, which Do mode currently does not receive.
notes: Medium confidence: only the loader and runner headers were read this pass; field list is from the scout inventory.

name: Typed HTTP API plus WebSocket RPC as a de facto SDK for third-party clients
what: Anything the desktop UI does can be done by another client that pairs with the server: the same typed contracts are reachable over HTTP (snapshots, dispatch, auth) and WebSocket.
how: EnvironmentHttpApi groups: descriptor (/.well-known/t3/environment), auth (session, browser-session, /oauth/token, websocket-ticket, pairing credential and links, clients, revoke), orchestration (snapshot, shell snapshot, thread snapshot by id, dispatch), pull-requests diff, connect (link-proof, relay-config, link-state, unlink, preferences, health, mint-credential). Bearer or DPoP tokens carry scopes; the CORS layer allows any origin for GET/POST/OPTIONS with authorization, dpop, traceparent and b3 headers so a hosted web client (app.t3.codes) can attach to a user's server.
verevonRelevance: Verevon exposes its APIs through a BFF; publishing a stable, scoped, typed external API (plus pairing for companion apps) is the route to the plugin/app ecosystem the references (Codex, Manus) have.
notes: No public documentation of the API was found in the app; it is internal-contract-first.

name: Dual-stream NDJSON provider logs (native and canonical) with rotation, batching and retention caps
what: Every provider session writes what the agent really sent (native) and what T3 normalized it to (canonical), per thread, to rotating files, so any rendering bug can be traced to a protocol message.
how: ProviderEventLoggers owns one shared EventNdjsonLogStore with views native, canonical and orchestration. Writers batch for 1 s, cap buffers at 1 MiB/512 records, rotate at 10 MiB across 10 files per thread, enforce a 512 MiB total and 14-day age with a 5 minute retention check, and skip transient canonical event types (content.delta, item.updated, task.progress, tool.progress, hook.progress, realtime audio, proposed deltas). Multiple provider instances share the same store to avoid rotation races; logging failures never block startup.
verevonRelevance: Directly supports Verevon's transparency goals: persist raw provider frames and canonical events side by side per run with bounded retention (subject to ZDR flags), exposed in a debug view.
notes: These logs contain prompts and tool output on the user's disk; ZDR-style products would need per-tenant redaction or an off switch.

name: Local trace file plus OTLP export, browser trace ingest and in-app trace diagnostics
what: Server spans are always written to a rotating local NDJSON file and optionally exported over OTLP; browser spans are forwarded through the server; and an in-app diagnostics view summarizes recent failures and slow spans.
how: ObservabilityLive builds a local file tracer (serverTracePath, traceMaxBytes, traceMaxFiles, batch window) with an optional OtlpTracer delegate and OtlpMetrics (counters and timers: t3_rpc_requests_total, t3_orchestration_command_ack_duration, t3_provider_turn_duration, t3_git_command_duration, t3_terminal_sessions_total and others), HTTP header redaction, and BrowserTraceCollector fed by POST /api/observability/v1/traces (operate scope) which also proxies to the OTLP URL when set. TraceDiagnostics parses the local trace file into span summaries, recent failures and log events for server.getTraceDiagnostics. The desktop has its own rotating logs (10 MiB x 10) and per-backend child logs.
verevonRelevance: Verevon can offer admins a per-run trace view built from its existing OTel data and show recent-failure summaries in the product, not only in Grafana.
notes: Rare to see a consumer app surface its own trace diagnostics to the user.

name: Usage and cost computed from provider transcripts (ccusage approach) with priced buckets
what: The usage page reflects what the agent CLIs actually did, including turns driven outside T3, priced from a public price table.
how: UsageService scans the provider tools' own .jsonl transcripts modified in the window (30-day scans over about 1.4 GB in 2-3 s cold), memoises parsed records by (size, mtime) with an on-disk scan cache and a 36 h mtime slack, dedupes within files (message/request pair), buckets by hour/day/model/provider and prices input, output, cache-read and cache-creation tokens from LiteLLM's model_prices_and_context_window.json (24 h TTL) at the base tier only (the transcripts do not record the serving tier, so tiered, flex, priority and batch rates are deliberately ignored), while discounting history copied into forked or subagent rollouts with a 1 s gap rule. server.getUsageSummary returns a UsageSummary with a contract version.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's cost-core records authoritative per-call cost; the useful addition is a user-facing, hourly/daily/model bucketed usage view and a price table with a documented tiering rule.
notes: The path was read as code only; no transcript files were opened. Reading another tool's private session files is only acceptable on a user-owned machine.

name: Four runtime modes with provider-specific translation, defaulting to full access
what: One permission vocabulary (approval-required, auto-accept-edits, auto, full-access) is translated for each agent; the default for new threads is full access.
how: orchestration.ts defines RuntimeMode and DEFAULT_RUNTIME_MODE = full-access. Translations: Claude to permissionMode default/acceptEdits/auto/bypassPermissions (with allowDangerouslySkipPermissions); Codex to approvalPolicy untrusted/on-request/never with sandbox read-only/workspace-write/danger-full-access and an explicit approvals reviewer (auto_review for auto); OpenCode to a PermissionRuleset; ACP agents to mode aliases plus auto-approving allow options in full-access. Switching mode restarts the provider session (ensureSessionForThread compares desired and current mode). Providers without an AI reviewer fall back to supervised behavior for auto.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's capability policy is stricter (ask posture, HITL); keep its defaults, but adopt the idea of a small, user-visible mode vocabulary that is mechanically translated per runtime.
notes: Corrects the scout (three modes, not four). The full-access default is the riskiest default among the apps audited.

name: Human-versus-agent control arbitration in the shared browser tab
what: The user can grab the mouse or keyboard in the preview at any time. The app distinguishes the agent's own synthetic input from the human's, shows who is in control, and aborts the agent's in-flight action when the human acts.
how: Before each synthetic click or key the manager records an expected input signal for the tab (expires after 1 s). The guest preload reports real input over HUMAN_INPUT_CHANNEL; handleHumanInput consumes a matching expected signal (agent) or otherwise bumps a per-tab control epoch, sets controller 'human' and resets it to 'none' after 750 ms. withControlSession checks the epoch so a running action fails with PreviewAutomationControlInterruptedError (message: interrupted by human input), while cleanup commands (key up, focus emulation off) still run so Chromium is not left with a held key. Tab state carries controller human, agent or none for the UI.
verevonRelevance: Verevon has live frames and manual takeover in Quarry/BFF but no Model Plane path; an epoch-based interrupt (human input invalidates the running agent action and the UI shows the current controller) is the right primitive for safe takeover.
notes: REA observed the HUMAN_INPUT_CHANNEL send in preview-pick-preload.cjs line 1588 and 1597. The mechanism is time-window based (1 s expectation), so a human action that exactly matches an expected synthetic signal within the window would be ignored.

name: Model catalogs by protocol: static Claude list gated by installed CLI version, live Codex list, ACP config options for Cursor and Grok
what: Each agent's models and their tunable options (reasoning effort, fast mode, thinking, context window) are discovered the way that agent exposes them, then normalized into one capability descriptor the picker and the adapters share.
how: ClaudeProvider ships a static catalog (claude-opus-5 with a 1M variant, opus 4.8/4.7/4.6/4.5, sonnet 5 and 4.6, haiku 4.5, fable-5) and filters entries by comparing the installed Claude Code version against per-model minimum versions with compareSemverVersions; CodexProvider pages through the app-server model/list request until nextCursor is empty; CursorProvider and Grok run a short ACP probe (clientInfo t3-code-provider-probe) and build capabilities from session config options (reasoning effort, context, fast, thinking). At session start the Claude adapter resolves capabilities for the chosen model, validates effort, maps ultracode to xhigh plus a settings flag, and only sets fastMode or thinking when the descriptor offers them. Codex service tier and fast mode share one option helper.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's router needs per-model capability descriptors too; the pattern 'discover live where possible, ship a version-gated static list otherwise, expose one descriptor' avoids hard-coding option UIs per provider.
notes: The sibling UI audit covers how descriptors render in the picker (its records 004-011). Model identifiers such as claude-opus-5 and claude-fable-5 come from the shipped catalog.

name: In-process native workspace index with strict time and size budgets
what: File and content search for @-mentions and the project search dialog is served by a native file index that runs inside the server process, with hard limits so a huge repo cannot stall the UI.
how: WorkspaceSearchIndex wraps @ff-labs/fff-node FileFinder (a C-ABI native library) per workspace root: it indexes up to 25,000 entries, aborts a scan after 15 s, evicts idle indexes after 15 minutes, caps content search at 250 ms and 100 matches per file and returns cursor-paged mixed (file and directory) results; searchRanking in shared ranks results. WorkspaceEntries refreshes the index after revert or file mutations.
verevonRelevance: Space-scoped file search in Verevon's sandbox workspace could use the same budgeted, cursor-paged index (in Rust, the ignore and nucleo crates are the analogue).
notes: Medium confidence: only the constants and imports were read. The native library is a dependency to replace in a Rust port.

name: Layered path containment: lexical resolution plus realpath checks at I/O sites
what: Reading and writing project files, serving workspace assets and reading workflow scripts all refuse paths that escape the allowed root, including through symlinks.
how: WorkspacePaths.resolveRelativePathWithinRoot rejects absolute paths and results that are empty, '.', '..' or start with '../' after path.relative. WorkspaceFileSystem additionally takes realpath of the workspace root and of the target before writing (operations realpath-workspace-root and realpath-target) and writes atomically via temp file and rename. AssetAccess canonicalizes with fileSystem.realPath and only issues tokens for files under the canonical workspace root. workflowScriptQuery requires the resolved realpath to live under ~/.claude/projects. ReviewService canonicalizes cwd and requires it within the workspace or worktrees root. The attachments directory is granted to the agent as a leaf directory only.
verevonRelevance: Same checks are required in Verevon's workspace promotion and sandbox file APIs; the combination of lexical normalization with realpath at the point of use is the safe pattern.
notes: The lexical resolver alone would not stop a symlink inside the workspace pointing outside; the realpath step at write time is what covers that.

name: Short-lived HMAC capability URLs for workspace images, previews and favicons
what: Files the browser needs (workspace images, HTML previews, project icons) are served through signed, expiring URLs instead of an authenticated path API, so an tag can load them without custom headers.
how: AssetAccess creates claims {kind, workspace or attachment id, relative path, expiresAt} base64url-encoded and signed with HMAC using a 32-byte random key stored in the secret store (asset-access-signing-key), producing /api/assets/<payload.signature>/<file>. Tokens live 1 hour (project favicon tokens are bucketed to 30 minutes for cache stability); resolveAsset verifies the signature with a timing-safe comparison, re-checks canonical paths and file types and only serves allowlisted preview extensions. Issuance goes through the authenticated assets.createUrl RPC.
verevonRelevance: Verevon artifacts in MinIO and workspace files need the same short-lived signed capability links for the SPA and for shared previews; reuse the claim structure (kind, scope, path, expiry) and a rotating key.
notes: CORS is wildcard origin for the whole API; the protection is authorization, not origin.

name: Runtime-fetched control data: what is pinned and what is trusted blindly
what: At runtime the server and CLI pull data and code from the network. Some of it is pinned by hash, some is only schema-gated, and one item is free-text that steers a coding agent.
how: Pinned: cloudflared binaries (URL plus SHA-256 per platform, verified before install), the service launcher's pinned t3@version runtimes (exact versions, preflight before activation). Schema-gated but unauthenticated: model-manifest.json from the main branch of the T3 repository (version literal, schema decoded, only reclassifies models) and LiteLLM's price table (24 h TTL; shapes narrowed to the fields read). Unpinned free text: the triage playbook, which the playbook prompt instructs the agent to fetch from the main branch. Telemetry goes to PostHog. Provider CLI updates query the package registry.
verevonRelevance: A checklist for Verevon's own runtime data dependencies (model tables, prompts, tool manifests): pin by digest, sign, or ship with the build; never let remote text steer an agent unreviewed.
notes: INF: the classification of trust is my judgement from the code (the individual fetches are SRC). The triage playbook was not fetched in this audit.

name: Guarded kill switch for runaway processes with stale-identity and ancestry checks
what: The diagnostics page can signal a process, but only one that is still the same process and a descendant of the T3 backend; the server never signals itself.
how: server.getProcessDiagnostics lists the backend's process tree with elapsed time and resource data from the native monitor; server.signalProcess takes {pid, startTimeMs, signal}, refreshes the process table, refuses when the pid is the server process, when the pid's start time no longer matches (stale identity) or when it is not a descendant of the backend, then calls process.kill. The RPC requires the operate scope.
verevonRelevance: Good model for a user-facing 'stop this process' control in Verevon's background process tools: identity pinning by start time prevents PID reuse mistakes.
notes: Scope is coarse (operate), but the per-call guards are strong.

name: Settings and keybindings as hot-reloaded files, with sensitive provider variables split into the secret store
what: The two user-editable config files take effect when edited outside the app, and API keys or other sensitive environment variables for provider instances never live in settings.json.
how: ServerSettings uses a capacity-1 cache, a semaphore and FileSystem.watch for external edit detection, writes atomically via temp directory plus rename, and runs the file through a schema with decoding defaults. Provider instance environment variables flagged sensitive are written to the secret store (providerEnvironmentSecretName per instance and variable) and materialized only when building a provider; clients receive redactServerSettingsForClient output where values are blank with valueRedacted true. Keybindings reload from keybindings.json with a 100 ms debounce on watch events (editors emit several events per save) and an RPC to upsert or remove a rule.
verevonRelevance: For Verevon's configuration surface (organization and Space settings), mark fields sensitive in the schema and split them to a secret store automatically, returning redacted values to clients.
notes: Matches the 'highly customizable and transparent' goal: everything is a readable file and a typed RPC. The secrets in the store are plaintext files (see the secret store record).

name: No T3-owned memory; provider-owned memory and instructions pass through, and Codex memory-consolidation threads are hidden
what: T3 has no long-term memory, user model or learning loop. It lets each agent use its own memory and instruction files and keeps the agents' background memory jobs out of the visible timeline.
how: The Claude adapter loads user, project and local setting sources so CLAUDE.md and the user's settings apply. The Codex shadow home keeps log, memories and tmp local per instance. CodexSessionRuntime filters notifications and threads whose source is memory_consolidation so background memory consolidation does not appear as chat. Personalization is limited to settings, favorites, accent colors, themes and keybindings.
verevonRelevance: A clear gap in this reference and a place where Verevon (Letta bridge, Dreaming) already leads; do not copy, but note that surfacing a provider's own memory jobs as quiet background activity is a good UX.
notes: Absence claim: based on keyword and structure searches in the recovered server source (no memory service, store or tools); the scout reached the same conclusion.

name: Web search and research are delegated to the agents; T3 only renders the tool items
what: T3 provides no search, browsing-for-answers, citation or research mode of its own. When an agent uses a search tool, the event is normalized to a web_search item and shown in the timeline.
how: Claude WebSearch and ACP web tool kinds map to the canonical web_search item type (one of seven tool lifecycle types); there are no search providers, source cards or research orchestrations in the server. The built-in preview browser is for the user and for browser automation tools, not for grounding answers.
verevonRelevance: Confirms T3 is not a research competitor; Verevon's in-gateway deep research and citation work is a differentiator versus this reference.
notes: Absence claim; the scout reached the same conclusion.

name: State directory layout and ownership map
what: Everything the server persists sits under one base directory with a clear layout, so backup, diagnosis, multi-instance isolation and uninstall are simple.
how: deriveServerPaths: <base>/userdata (or dev/ when a dev URL is set without explicit base) holds state.sqlite (+wal/shm), settings.json, keybindings.json, attachments/, logs/ (server.log, server.trace.ndjson, provider/events.log, terminals/*.log), anonymous-id, environment-id, server-runtime.json and secrets/ (0700); <base>/caches holds provider status caches; <base>/worktrees holds managed worktrees; <base>/runtime/versions holds pinned runtimes for the boot service; relay client binaries install under the base dir. The desktop keeps its own userData (t3code or t3code-dev) with desktop-settings.json, client-settings.json, saved-environments.json and an encrypted connection catalog, and a separate WSL backend has its own Linux home.
verevonRelevance: A reminder to define a single, documented data-ownership map for any local companion; for the hosted plane the equivalent is the per-plane database ownership already enforced by the no-cross-plane-DB rule.
notes: No user data files were read; only path derivation code.

name: Monorepo layering: contracts, shared, client-runtime and protocol packages under thin apps
what: The code base is organized so that wire contracts and protocol clients are standalone packages that the desktop, server and web app all depend on, keeping apps thin.
how: pnpm workspace with apps (desktop, server, web) and packages: contracts (Effect Schema wire types for rpc, ipc, orchestration, settings, provider, preview, terminal, git/vcs, pull requests, relay, usage and more), shared (git, shell, keybindings, preview, relay JWT, semver, qr code, observability helpers), client-runtime (connection, authorization, rpc session, relay discovery, persistence), effect-acp, effect-codex-app-server, ssh, tailscale; a mobile app exists in the monorepo (Expo/React Native overrides) but is not in this build. Dependencies are pinned by pnpm overrides and patches (Effect 4.0.0-beta.103, @effect/atom-react, a patched virtual-list library, vite-plus).
verevonRelevance: Verevon's monorepo already splits planes; the transferable rule is that wire contracts and protocol clients must be packages with no app imports so the SPA, gateway and tools cannot drift.
notes: Medium confidence: workspace layout is from the scout inventory and package directories; pnpm-workspace.yaml was not re-read in this pass.

name: Rust-portability assessment of the T3 architecture
what: Which parts of T3's architecture map cleanly onto a Rust implementation (Verevon's Model Plane is Rust and Go) and which parts exist only because of Node, Electron or Effect.
how: Portable as-is in concept: the pure decider and projector functions over events; command receipts; the canonical runtime event schema; JSON-RPC over stdio clients generated from published schemas (Codex app-server, ACP); SQLite or Postgres projection tables with per-projector cursors; NDJSON logs with rotation; demand-lease background policy; DPoP and scoped-token auth; the launcher/trial/rollback update protocol; the Rust sidecar protocol (already Rust). Needs replacement: Effect layers (use traits plus a supervisor), node-pty (portable-pty), the native file index (ignore plus a matcher crate), Electron shell pieces (Tauri or none for web), the Playwright injected-script extraction (a different perception layer such as CDP accessibility snapshots), Clerk/Electron bridges. Better in Rust: the resource monitor and any hot-path event fan-out with bounded channels.
verevonRelevance: Use as the porting checklist when Verevon recreates the Claude-desktop-style runtime features in Rust.
notes: INF: basis is the module structure and dependencies read in this audit; no Rust prototype was built.

name: Distribution layout: two ASAR archives, unpacked natives, sidecar executable and a GitHub-release update feed
what: The installed app is a small Electron shell archive plus a separate, larger server archive, a native resource monitor and an elevation helper; updates come from GitHub releases for the repository owner.
how: resources/ contains app.asar (91.6 MB: apps/desktop plus node_modules including effect, Clerk, Playwright core, undici), server.asar (130.5 MB: apps/server with the built SPA in dist/client, node-pty prebuilds, fff natives), app.asar.unpacked and server.asar.unpacked/node_modules for native modules that cannot run from an archive, resource-monitor/t3-resource-monitor.exe and elevate.exe (an installer elevation helper). app-update.yml configures electron-updater with provider github, owner pingdotgg, repo t3code, releaseType release, a dedicated updater cache directory and a publisherName allow-list. The server runs from the archive via ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE (asar-aware); the WSL backend needs a loose copy, extracted on demand.
verevonRelevance: None for a hosted product; relevant only if Verevon ships a desktop companion, where the 'shell archive plus server archive' split lets the engine update on its own cadence.
notes: File sizes were read from the install folder listing (91,615,439 and 130,516,741 bytes). The publisherName entry implies signature publisher verification by electron-updater on Windows (INF: library behavior, not read in this audit).

name: Test seams built into production code: injectable loggers, mock update server and in-memory database layer
what: Production modules expose small hooks so tests can run without the real network, filesystem or provider processes.
how: ProviderServiceLiveOptions lets tests swap the canonical event logger and the MCP credential issue/revoke functions (so the agent-browser gate is observable); DesktopConfig reads T3CODE_DESKTOP_MOCK_UPDATES and a mock server port so the updater can point at a local generic feed; Sqlite.ts exports SqlitePersistenceMemory (':memory:' with the same migrations and pragmas); ServerConfig has layerTest(cwd, baseDir or prefix); PreviewAutomationBroker and McpSessionRegistry take clock and options parameters; ProviderEventLoggers has NoOpProviderEventLoggers; RuntimeReceiptBus publishes checkpoint-baseline, diff-finalized and turn-quiesced receipts that exist only so tests can wait for exact milestones (streamEventsForTest), and DrainableWorker.drain replaces timing-based sleeps. fast-check ships in the desktop dependency list.
verevonRelevance: For the Model Plane: keep clocks, ID generators and network clients injectable so failure paths (credential revocation, restart recovery) are unit-testable.
notes: The test hooks are env-gated, so a user could enable the mock update server by environment; they are dev/test hooks, not security controls.

name: Per-instance harness customization: binary path, launch arguments, home, environment variables and custom models
what: Every provider instance can be pointed at a specific binary, started with extra arguments, run with its own config home and environment, and extended with custom model names, which makes the harness adjustable without code changes.
how: Settings per instance carry binaryPath, launchArgs, homePath/shadowHomePath, environment variables (with a sensitive flag) and customModels. The Claude adapter parses launchArgs with parseCliArgs and passes them as extraArgs to the SDK; Codex builds app-server args from launchArgs and lets T3CODE_CODEX_LAUNCH_ARGS override them; mergeProviderInstanceEnvironment layers instance variables over the process environment; custom model lists extend the picker. Binary paths resolve through the login-shell-hydrated PATH.
verevonRelevance: Matches the 'highly customizable harness' goal: expose per-runtime launch parameters, env and extra models as typed, auditable settings rather than code.
notes: No UI to edit MCP servers or hooks exists; customization is via CLI flags and env, which assumes a technical user.

name: Plugin and MCP lifecycle events pass through, but T3 has no plugin or MCP management of its own
what: When an agent installs a plugin or an MCP server reports status or an OAuth completion, T3 receives the event and shows it, but T3 itself offers no marketplace, manifest or MCP configuration surface.
how: ClaudeAdapter maps the SDK plugin_install system message to a runtime event; the canonical taxonomy includes mcp.status.updated and mcp.oauth.completed and an mcp_elicitation_approval request type that routes MCP prompts through the approval UI; the Codex app-server client has plugin/marketplace/mcpServer methods in its generated schema that T3 does not call (it only calls config/mcpServer/reload after registering its own server).
verevonRelevance: A gap Verevon can exploit: Codex's plugin, marketplace and MCP APIs exist in the app-server protocol Verevon already speaks, and T3 leaves them unused, so a first-class plugin surface is a differentiator.
notes: Consistent with the sibling audit: 'no user-facing MCP/plugin management'.

name: Zero-install web launch: running `t3` in a repo auto-creates the project and a thread and opens a one-time pairing URL
what: Running the CLI from a project directory starts the server, registers that directory as a project (or finds the existing one), makes sure it has a thread, and opens the browser at a URL that carries a one-time pairing credential.
how: With autoBootstrapProjectFromCwd, resolveAutoBootstrapWelcomeTargets looks up the active project by workspace root, creates it via project.create (title from the folder name, default model selection) when missing, then ensures the first active thread exists or dispatches thread.create (default interaction mode, runtime mode full-access), and publishes a 'welcome' lifecycle event with the bootstrap project and thread ids. resolveStartupBrowserTarget issues a startup pairing URL (issueStartupPairingUrl) in non-desktop mode and maybeOpenBrowser launches it unless --no-browser. The CLI detects how it was launched (npx, pnpm dlx, bunx) to print matching follow-up commands.
verevonRelevance: Onboarding lesson for Verevon: open directly into a ready-to-type workspace with a pre-created thread and a credentialed link; no empty states or setup wizard.
notes: The new thread defaults to full-access runtime mode.

name: Account sign-in through Clerk's Electron bridge (token cache, OAuth transport, passkeys), gated by a build-time key
what: Signing in to T3 Connect uses Clerk with native bridges for token storage, OAuth redirects and passkeys, and exists only in builds that carry a Clerk publishable key.
how: DesktopClerk configures the @clerk/electron bridge for the state directory and derives the Clerk frontend API hostname from a build-time constant (__T3CODE_BUILD_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY__) to extend the CSP; passkeys are enabled. REA found two contextBridge APIs for Clerk (__clerk_internal_electron and __clerk_internal_electron_passkeys) and Clerk channels for token cache get/save/clear, OAuth transport open/getRedirectUrl and passkey create/get/capabilities. CLI login uses OAuth PKCE (loopback or out-of-band code prompt) and stores the refreshed token in the server secret store.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's Control Plane already owns identity, orgs and SSO; T3 shows only consumer sign-in, so it is a negative reference for enterprise requirements.
notes: The relay and connect features are unavailable in builds without public configuration (CLI text). No SSO, SAML or org model exists.

name: Reasoning effort, fast mode and thinking as per-model descriptors applied live to a running session
what: Effort, fast mode and thinking are exposed only when the selected model's descriptor offers them, and a change applies to the live session without restarting it.
how: ClaudeAdapter reads getClaudeModelCapabilities(model) and getProviderOptionDescriptors, resolves effort with resolveClaudeEffort, enables fastMode and thinking only when a boolean descriptor with that id exists, and maps the special ultracode effort to xhigh plus settings.ultracode. On later turns it compares the API model id and calls query.setModel when it differs and recomputes current effort; context-window selection comes from selectedClaudeContextWindow. Codex service tier and fast mode share getCodexServiceTierOptionValue; ACP agents change options through session/set_config_option with value validation (validateConfigOptionValue) and session/set_model.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's cost-aware intent router and per-model options could share one descriptor so the SPA can expose reasoning controls that apply mid-conversation.
notes: Complements the catalog record; the sibling audit covers the picker UI.

name: Live shell stream: attach before snapshot, coalesce per aggregate, refetch the projection, resume from the client's sequence
what: The sidebar stream stays correct and cheap under bursts of events. Many events for one thread collapse into a single re-read of that thread's summary, and a client that already holds a snapshot only receives what it missed.
how: subscribeShell first attaches a scope-bound live buffer on streamDomainEvents (so nothing published during the snapshot query is lost), then loads the shell snapshot or, when the client passes its snapshot sequence, replays shell events after it. Live events pass through coalesceShellLiveStream, a keyed worker that keeps only the latest value per key (KeyedCoalescingWorker with drainKey), so high-frequency events (message deltas, activity appends) become one refetch per aggregate per window. toShellStreamEvent maps events to project-upserted/removed or thread-upserted/removed by refetching the projection row (retry once; a persistence error is logged and dropped rather than treated as a missing row); a removal is emitted when the refetch returns none, which stays correct when a burst collapses a delete into a later event. A 'synchronized' completion marker is offered into the same queue so everything buffered is delivered before the client is told it is in sync. Clients dedupe by sequence. A small helper (subscribeBeforeSnapshot, with a mutex form that serializes snapshot then subscribe and a no-mutex form that subscribes first) provides the snapshot/subscription handoff for other streams.
verevonRelevance: Verevon's SSE and NATS fan-out can adopt the same recipe: treat events as invalidation triggers, coalesce per aggregate, refetch from the projection, and attach the live tail before loading the snapshot to avoid the classic gap.
notes: The sibling UI audit describes the client half (snapshot then resume, dedupe by sequence); this record documents the server's race-free ordering and coalescing.

name: Thread deletion cascade through a reactor, and what it leaves behind
what: Deleting a thread stops its agent session and closes its terminals including their saved history. Other per-thread artifacts are handled elsewhere or not at all.
how: ThreadDeletionReactor listens on the domain event stream for thread.deleted, enqueues into a drainable worker, calls providerService.stopSession and terminalManager.close({deleteHistory: true}) with best-effort logging of failures (interrupts propagate). A search of the server source finds checkpoint refs deleted only by the revert path (CheckpointReactor) and attachments deleted only by the client-driven attachments.delete RPC or the pending-attachment sweep; no thread-deletion path removes the hidden refs/t3/checkpoints/<thread>/... refs or the thread's worktree.
verevonRelevance: A deletion-cascade checklist item for Verevon (runs, child runs, sandbox leases, artifacts, memory, ZDR purge): make every per-thread resource owner subscribe to the deletion event and test that nothing is left behind.
notes: The 'left behind' part is INF from absence of calls in the code read (medium confidence); it was not verified at runtime. Hidden git refs are cheap but accumulate in the user's repository.

name: Cross-environment repository identity from the normalized git remote
what: The same repository gets the same identity key wherever it is cloned (local disk, WSL, an SSH host), so projects and pull requests can be grouped and matched across environments.
how: RepositoryIdentityResolver runs git remote -v for a cwd, prefers the upstream then origin fetch URL (else the first remote alphabetically), normalizes it with normalizeGitRemoteUrl into a canonicalKey (host/owner/name), detects the source-control provider from the URL, and returns {canonicalKey, locator{source git-remote, remoteName, remoteUrl}, rootPath, displayName, provider, owner, name}; results are cached (512 entries, 1 minute positive and negative TTL). Every client-side reference is scoped by environment (ScopedProjectRef, ScopedThreadRef carry environmentId) because ids are unique only per environment.
verevonRelevance: Verevon Spaces that point at the same external repository or document set could carry a canonical identity key so grouping, de-duplication and cross-plane references do not depend on per-plane ids.
notes: Capability is advertised in the descriptor (repositoryIdentity) so older servers are not probed.
